3. SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES
3.1 Cash and cash equivalents
Cash and cash equivalents comprise cash on hand, cash at banks and short-term, highly liquid investments with an original 
maturity of less than three months that are readily convertible into known amounts of cash and that are subject to an 
insignificant risk of change in value.
3.2 Inventories
Inventories are stated at the lower of cost incurred in bringing each product to its present location and condition, and net 
realisable value. Net realisable value represents the estimated selling price in the ordinary course of business less the 
estimated costs to complete and the estimated costs necessary to make the sale.
The perpetual method is used to record inventories, which are valued as follows:
Raw materials and consumables 
- cost of purchase on a weighted average basis.
Finished goods and work in process
- cost of direct materials and labour plus attributable 
manufacturing overheads based on the normal operating 
capacity on a weighted average basis.
Provision for obsolete inventories
An inventory provision is created for the estimated loss arising due to the impairment of value (through diminution, damage, 
obsolescence, etc.) of raw materials, finished goods, and other inventories owned by the Group, based on appropriate 
evidence of impairment available at the balance sheet date.
Increases or decreases to the provision balance are recorded into the cost of goods sold account in the consolidated income 
statement.
3.3 Receivables
Receivables are presented in the consolidated financial statements at the carrying amounts due from customers and other 
debtors, after provision for doubtful debts.
The provision for doubtful debts represents amounts of outstanding receivables at the balance sheet date which are doubtful 
of being recovered. Increases or decreases to the provision balance are recorded as general and administrative expense in 
the consolidated income statement.
3.4 Tangible fixed assets
Tangible fixed assets are stated at cost less accumulated depreciation.
The cost of a tangible fixed asset comprises its purchase price and any directly attributable costs of bringing the tangible 
fixed asset to working condition for its intended use.
Expenditures for additions, improvements and renewals are added to the carrying amount of the assets and expenditures 
for maintenance and repairs are charged to the consolidated income statement as incurred.
When tangible fixed assets are sold or retired, any gain or loss resulting from their disposal (the difference between the net 
disposal proceeds and the carrying amount) is included in the consolidated income statement.
3.5 Intangible assets
Intangible assets are stated at cost less accumulated amortisation.
The cost of an intangible asset comprises its purchase price and any directly attributable costs of preparing the intangible 
asset for its intended use.
Expenditures for additions, improvements are added to the carrying amount of the assets and other expenditures are 
charged to the consolidated income statement as incurred.
When intangible assets are sold or retired, any gain or loss resulting from their disposal (the difference between the net 
disposal proceeds and the carrying amount) is included in the consolidated income statement.
Land use rights (“LURs”)
LURs are recorded as intangible assets if the land is held for use in the production and business or for rent to others by 
the Group and when the Group receives the LUR certificate. The cost of LUR comprises any directly attributable costs of 
preparing the land for its intended use. Land with indefinite useful file is not amortised.
The advance payment for land rental, of which the land lease contracts have effectiveness prior to 2003 and land use right 
certificate being issued, are recorded as intangible asset according to Circular No. 45/2013/TT-BTC issued by the Ministry 
of Finance on 25 April 2013 providing guideline for the management, use and calculation of depreciation or amortisation of 
assets (“Circular 45”).
Copyrights
Copyrights of maize and rice varieties are recognized at the purchase price for varieties not researched and developed by 
the Company and its subsidiaries. Copyrights are amortized on a straight-line basis over the short period of time between 
the estimated useful life and the time of purchase.
3.6 Depreciation and amortisation
Depreciation of tangible fixed assets and amortisation of intangible assets are calculated on a straight-line basis over the 
estimated useful life of each asset as follows:
Buildings and structures
5 - 25 years
Machineries and equipment 
3 - 10 years
Means of transportation
3 - 20 years
Office equipment 
3 - 10 years
Land use rights with definite useful life 
10 - 50 years
Copyrights
5 years
Computer software 
3 - 6 years
Others
5 - 8 years
3.7 Borrowing costs
Borrowing costs consist of interest and other costs that the Group incurs in connection with the borrowing of funds and are 
recorded as expense during the period in which they are incurred, except to the extent that they are capitalized as explained 
in the following paragraph.
Borrowing costs that are directly attributable to the acquisition, construction or production of an asset that necessarily take 
a substantial period of time to get ready for its intended use or sale are capitalized as part of the cost of the respective asset.

3.8 Investment properties
Investment properties are stated at cost including transaction costs less accumulated depreciation. Investment properties 
held for capital appreciation are not amortised but subject to impairment review.
Subsequent expenditure relating to an investment property that has already been recognized is added to the net book value 
of the investment property when it is probable that future economic benefits, in excess of the originally assessed standard 
of performance of the existing investment property.
Depreciation of investment properties are calculated on a straight-line basis over the estimated useful life of each asset as 
follows:
Buildings and structures
5 - 20 years
Others
6 - 15 years
Investment properties are derecognised when either they have been disposed of or when the investment properties are 
permanently withdrawn from use and no future economic benefit is expected from its disposal. The difference between the 
net disposal proceeds and the carrying amount of the assets is recognised in the consolidated income statement in the year 
of retirement or disposal.
Transfers are made to investment properties when, and only when, there is a change in use, evidenced by ending of owner-
occupation, commencement of an operating lease to another party or ending of construction or development. Transfers are 
made from investment properties when, and only when, there is change in use, evidenced by commencement of owner-
occupation or commencement of development with a view to sale. The transfer from investment property to owner-occupied 
property or inventories does not change the cost or the carrying value of the property for subsequent accounting at the date 
of change in use.
3.9 Leased assets
The determination of whether an arrangement is, or contains a lease is based on the substance of the arrangement at 
inception date and requires an assessment of whether the fulfilment of the arrangement is dependent on the use of specific 
assets and the arrangement conveys a right to use the asset.
Leases are classified as finance leases whenever the terms of the lease transfer substantially all the risks and rewards of 
ownership of the asset to the lessee. All other leases are classified as operating leases.
Where the Group is the lessee
Rentals under operating leases are charged to the consolidated income statement on a straight-line basis over the lease 
term.
Where the Group is the lessor
Assets subject to operating leases are included as the Group’s investment property in the consolidated balance sheet. Initial 
direct costs incurred in negotiating an operating lease are recognised in the consolidated income statement as incurred.
Lease income is recognised in the consolidated income statement on a straight-line basis over the lease term.
3.10	 Prepaid expenses
Prepaid expenses are reported as short-term or long-term prepaid expenses on the consolidated balance sheet and 
amortised over the period for which the amount are paid or the period in which economic benefit are generated in relation 
to these expenses.
Prepaid for land rental
The prepaid land rental represents the unamortised balance of advance payment made in accordance with lease contracts 
signed after 2003. Such prepaid rental is classified as long-term prepaid expenses for allocation to the consolidated 
income statement over the remaining lease period, according to Circular 45.
Fishery and fishery-related cost
Fishery and fishery-related cost include cost of renting ponds, digging ponds, replenishing ponds, and raising fish. The 
digging ponds, replenishing ponds, and raising fish costs are amortised over the year, in which economic benefits are 
generated in connection to the costs incurred.
3.11 Business combinations and goodwill
Business combinations are accounted for using the purchase method. The cost of a business combination is measured 
as the fair value of assets given, equity instruments issued and liabilities incurred or assumed at the date of exchange 
plus any costs directly attributable to the business combination. Identifiable assets and liabilities and contingent liabilities 
assumed in a business combination are measured initially at fair values at the date of business combination.
Goodwill is initially measured at cost being the excess of the cost of the business combination over the Group’s share in 
the net fair value of the acquiree’s identifiable assets, liabilities and contingent liabilities. If the cost of acquisition is less 
than the fair value of the net assets of the subsidiary acquired, the difference is recognized directly in the consolidated 
income statement. After initial recognition, goodwill is measured at cost less accumulated amortization. Amortization of 
goodwill is calculated on a straight-line basis over ten (10) years during which the source embodying economic benefits 
are recovered by the Group. The parent company conducts the periodical review for impairment of goodwill of investment 
in subsidiaries. If there are indicators of impairment loss incurred is higher than the yearly allocated amount of goodwill 
on the straight-line basis, the higher amount will be recorded in the consolidated income statement..
3.12 Investments
Investments in associates
The Group’s investment in its associates is accounted for using the equity method of accounting. An associate is an entity 
in which the Group has significant influence that is neither subsidiaries nor joint ventures. The Group generally deems they 
have significant influence if they have over 20% of the voting rights.
Under the equity method, the investment is carried in the consolidated balance sheet at cost plus post acquisition changes 
in the group’s share of net assets of the associates. Goodwill arising on acquisition of the associate is included in the 
carrying amount of the investment. Goodwill is not amortised and subject to annual review of impairment. The consolidated 
income statement reflects the share of the post-acquisition results of operation of the associates.
The share of post-acquisition profit (loss) of the associates is presented on face of the consolidated income statement 
and its share of post-acquisition movements in reserves is recognised in reserves. The cumulative post-acquisition 
movements are adjusted against the carrying amount of the investment. Dividend receivable from associates reduces the 
carrying amount of the investment.
The financial statements of the associates are prepared for the same reporting year and use the same accounting policies 
as the Group. Where necessary, adjustments are made to bring the accounting policies in line with those of the Group.
Held-for-trading securities and investments in other entities
Held-for-trading securities and investments in other entities are stated at their acquisition costs.

Provision for diminution in value of investments
Provision for diminution in value of investments
Provision of the investment is made when there are reliable evidences of the diminution in value of those investments at the 
balance sheet date. 
Increases or decreases to the provision balance are recorded as finance expenses in the consolidated income statement.
Held-to-maturity investments
Held-to-maturity investments are stated at their acquisition costs. After initial recognition, held-to-maturity investments 
are measured at recoverable amount. Any impairment loss incurred is recognised as finance expense in the consolidated 
income statement and deducted against the value of such investments.
3.13 Payable and accruals
Payable and accrual are recognised for amount to be paid in the future for goods and services received, whether or not billed 
to the Group.
3.14 Accrual for severance pay
The severance pay to employee is accrued at the end of each reporting year for all employees who have been in service for 
more than 12 months up to 31 December 2008 at the rate of one-half of the average monthly salary for each year of service 
up to 31 December 2008 in accordance with the Labor Code and related implementing guidance. The average monthly salary 
used in this calculation will be revised at the end of each reporting year following the average monthly salary of the 6-month 
period up to the reporting date.  Increases or decreases to the accrued amount other than actual payment to employee will 
be taken to the consolidated income statement.
This accrued severance pay is used to settle the termination allowance to be paid to employee upon termination of their 
labour contract following Article 48 of the Labor Code.
3.15 Foreign currency transactions
Transactions in currencies other than the Group’s reporting currency of VND are recorded at the actual transaction exchange 
rates at transaction dates which are determined as follows:
- Transaction resulting in receivables are recorded at the buying exchange rates of the commercial banks designated for 
collection; and
- Transactions resulting in liabilities are recorded at the selling exchange rates of the transaction of commercial banks 
designated for payment.
At the end of the year, monetary balances denominated in foreign currencies are translated at the actual transaction 
exchange rates at consolidated the balance sheet dates which are determined as follows:
- Monetary assets are translated at buying exchange rate of the commercial bank where the Group conducts transactions 
regularly; and
- Monetary liabilities are translated at selling exchange rate of the commercial bank where the Group conducts transactions 
regularly.
All foreign exchange differences incurred during the year and arising from the revaluation of monetary accounts denominated 
in foreign currency at year-end are taken to the consolidated income statement.
3.16 Appropriation of net profit 
Net profit after tax (excluding negative goodwill arising from a bargain purchase) is available for appropriation to investors 
after approval by appropriate level of authority, and after making appropriation to reserve funds in accordance with the 
Group’s Charter and Vietnamese regulatory requirements.
The Group maintains the following reserve funds which are appropriated from the Group’s net profit as proposed by the 
Board of Directors and subject to approval by shareholders at the Annual General Meeting.
Investment and development fund
This fund is set aside for use in the Group’s expansion of its operation or of in-depth investments.
Bonus and welfare fund
This fund is set aside for the purpose of pecuniary rewarding and encouraging, common benefits and improvement of the 
employees’ benefits, and presented as a liability on the consolidated balance sheet.
3.17 Treasury shares
Group’s own equity instruments which are reacquired (treasury shares) are recognised at cost and deducted from equity. No 
gain or loss is recognised in profit or loss upon purchase, sale, issue or cancellation of the Group’s own equity instruments.
3.18 Earnings per share
Basic earnings per share amounts are calculated by dividing net profit after tax for the year attributable to ordinary 
shareholders of the Group (after adjusting for the bonus and welfare fund) by the weighted average number of ordinary 
shares outstanding during the year.
Diluted earnings per share amounts are calculated by dividing the net profit after tax attributable to ordinary equity holders 
of the Group by the weighted average number of ordinary shares outstanding during the year plus the weighted average 
number of ordinary shares that would be issued on conversion of all the dilutive potential ordinary shares into ordinary 
shares.
3.19 Revenue recognition
Revenue is recognised to the extent that it is probable that the economic benefits will flow to the Group and the revenue can 
be reliably measured. Revenue is measured at the fair value of the consideration received or receivable, excluding trade 
discount, rebate and sales return. The following specific recognition criteria must also be met before revenue is recognised:
Sale of goods
Revenue is recognised when the significant risks and rewards of ownership of the goods have passed to the buyer, usually 
upon the delivery of the goods.
Rendering of services
Revenue is recognised when the services have been rendered and completed.
Interest
Revenue is recognised as the interest accrues (taking into account the effective yield on the asset) unless collectability is in 
doubt.
Dividends
Income is recognised when the Group’s entitlement as an investor to receive the dividend is established.

3.20 Taxation
Current income tax
Current income tax assets and liabilities for the current and prior years are measured at the amount expected to be 
recovered from or paid to the taxation authorities. The tax rates and tax laws used to compute the amount are those that are 
enacted as at the balance sheet date.
Current income tax is charged or credited to the consolidated income statement, except when it relates to items recognised 
directly to equity, in which case the current income tax is also dealt with in equity.
Current income tax assets and liabilities are offset when there is a legally enforceable right for the Group to offset current 
tax assets against current tax liabilities and when the Group intends to settle its current tax assets and liabilities on a net 
basis.
Deferred tax
TDeferred tax is provided using the liability method on temporary differences at the balance sheet date between the tax base 
of assets and liabilities and their carrying amount for financial reporting purposes.
Deferred tax liabilities are recognised for all taxable temporary differences, except:
- Where the deferred tax liability arises from the initial recognition of an asset or liability in a transaction which at the time 
of the related transaction affects neither the accounting profit nor taxable profit or loss; and
- In respect of taxable temporarily differences associated with investments in subsidiaries and associates where timing of 
the reversal of the temporary difference can be controlled and it is probable that the temporary difference will not reverse 
in the foreseeable future.
Deferred tax assets are recognised for all deductible temporary differences, carried forward unused tax credit and unused 
tax losses, to the extent that it is probable that taxable profit will be available against which deductible temporary differences, 
carried forward unused tax credit and unused tax losses can be utilised, except:
- Where the deferred tax asset in respect of deductible temporary difference which arises from the initial recognition of an 
asset or liability which at the time of the related transaction, affects neither the accounting profit nor taxable profit or loss; 
and
- In respect of deductible temporarily differences associated with investments in subsidiaries and associates, deferred tax 
assets are recognised only to the extent that it is probable that the temporary differences will reverse in the foreseeable 
future and taxable profit will be available against which the temporary differences can be utilised.
The carrying amount of deferred tax assets is reviewed at each balance sheet date and reduced to the extent that it is no 
longer probable that sufficient taxable profit will be available to allow all or part of the deferred income tax asset to be 
utilised. Previously unrecognised deferred tax assets are re-assessed at each balance sheet date and are recognised to the 
extent that it has become probable that future taxable profit will allow the deferred tax assets to be recovered.
Deferred tax assets and liabilities are measured at the tax rates that are expected to apply in the year when the asset 
realised or the liability is settled based on tax rates and tax laws that have been enacted or substantively enacted at the 
balance sheet date.
Deferred tax is charged or credited to the consolidated income statement, except when it relates to items recognised directly 
to equity, in which case the deferred tax is also dealt with in the equity account.
Deferred tax assets and liabilities are offset when there is a legally enforceable right for the Group to offset current tax 
assets against current tax liabilities and when they relate to income taxes levied by the same taxation authority on:
- Either the same taxable entity; or
- When the Group intends either settle current tax liabilities and assets on a net basis or to realise the assets and settle the 
liabilities simultaneously, in each future year in which significant amounts of deferred tax liabilities or assets are expected 
to be settled or recovered.
3.21 Financial instruments 
Financial instruments – initial recognition and presentation
Financial assets
Financial assets within the scope of Circular No. 210/TT-BTC issued by the Ministry of Finance on 6 November 2009 providing 
guidance for the adoption in Vietnam of the International Financial Reporting Standards on presentation and disclosures of 
financial instruments (“Circular 210”) are classified, for disclosures in the notes to the consolidated financial statements, as 
financial assets at fair value through profit or loss, held-to-maturity investments, loans and receivables or available-for-sale 
financial assets as appropriate. The Group determines the classification of its financial assets at initial recognition.
All financial assets are recognised initially at cost plus directly attributable transaction costs.
The Group’s financial assets include cash and cash equivalents, short-term trade receivables, other receivables and 
investments.
Financial liabilities
Financial liabilities within the scope of Circular 210 are classified, for disclosures in the notes to the consolidated financial 
statements, as financial liabilities at fair value through profit or loss or financial liabilities measured at amortised cost as 
appropriate. The Group determines the classification of its financial liabilities at initial recognition.
All financial liabilities are recognised initially at cost, net of directly attributable transaction costs.
The Group’s financial liabilities include short-term trade and other payables, accrued expenses and loans.
Financial instruments – subsequent re-measurement
There is currently no guidance in Circular 210 in relation to subsequent re-measurement of financial instruments. 
Accordingly, the financial instruments are subsequently re-measured at cost.
Offsetting of financial instruments
Financial assets and financial liabilities are offset and the net amount reported in the consolidated balance sheet if, and only 
if, there is a currently enforceable legal right to offset the recognised amounts and there is an intention to settle on a net 
basis, or to realise the assets and settle the liabilities simultaneously.
3.22 Segment information
A segment is a component determined separately by the Group which is engaged in providing products or related services 
(business segment) or providing products or services in a particular economic environment (geographical segment), that is 
subject to risks and returns that are different from those of other segments.
3.23 Related parties
Parties are considered to be related parties of the Group if one party has the ability to control the other party or exercise 
significant influence over the other party in making financial and operating decisions, or when the Group and other party are 
under common control or under common significant influence. Related parties can be enterprise or individual, including 
close members of the family of any such individual.

29.	 CORPORATE INCOME TAX
The Group has the obligation to pay corporate income tax (“CIT”) at the rate of 20% of taxable profits. In addition, the 
Company’s subsidiaries are entitled to the following CIT exemption and reductions:
- At ABT: According to Circular No. 96/2015/TT-BTC dated 22 June 2015 issued by Ministry of Finance and Official Letter 
No. 2200/CT-THNVDT dated 18 November 2015 issued by Department of Taxation of Ben Tre Province, ABT is entitled to 
preferential CIT over the entire operating period applied to incomes from cultivating aquacultures in disadvantage areas. 
Accordingly, CIT tax rate applied for profit from cultivating aquacultures activities from 2015 is 10%.
- At Vinaseed: On 1 March 2011, Vinaseed was approved as a scientific and technological enterprise through the Certificate 
No. 03/DK-DNKHCN issued by the Department of Science and Technology of Hanoi. According to the current regulations on 
scientific and technological enterprise and CIT incentives, Vinaseed shall be entitled to CIT exemption and reduction as a 
newly established enterprise from investment in the sector of high-tech, scientific research and technological development 
if revenues generated from scientific and technological products and goods for the first, second and third year exceed total 
revenue by 30%, 50% and 70%, respectively. In particular:
(i) The tax rate of 10% shall be applied for fifteen (15) years from the first year generated revenue from scientific and 
technological activities; and
(ii)  Vinaseed shall be exempted from CIT for a period of four (4) years and entitled to a 50% reduction of CIT payable for the 
subsequent nine (9) years.
- At SSC: On 30 July 2012, SSC was approved as a scientific and technological enterprise through the Certificate No. 08/
DK-DNKHCN issued by the Department of Science and Technology of Ho Chi Minh City. According to the current regulations 
on scientific and technological enterprise and CIT incentives, SSC shall be entitled to CIT exemption and reduction as newly 
established enterprise from investment in the sector of high-tech, scientific research and technological development if 
revenues generated from scientific and technological products and goods for the first, second and third year exceed total 
revenue by 30%, 50% and 70%, respectively. In particular:
(i) The tax rate of 10% shall be applied for fifteen years (15) from the first year generated revenue from scientific and 
technological activities; and
(ii) SSC shall be exempted from CIT for a period of four (4) years and entitled to a 50% reduction of CIT payable for the 
subsequent nine (9) years.
- At FMC: From the fiscal year ended 31 December 2015, the Company applied Circular No. 96/2015/TT-BTC dated 22 June 
2015 issued by Ministry of Finance of Vietnam providing guidelines for corporate income tax and the Official Letter No. 1327/
CT-TTr from Tax Department of Soc Trang Province on 1 December 2012. Details are as below:
(i) For agricultural and seafood activities in extremely disadvantaged areas: the Company is entitled to corporate income tax 
(“CIT”) exemption over the entire period; and
(ii) For seafood activities in disadvantaged areas: the Company is entitled to CIT at the rate of 10% over the entire period.
The other subsidiaries have the obligation to pay CIT at the rate of 20% of taxable profits.
The tax returns filed by Group are subject to examination by the tax authorities. As the application of tax laws and regulations 
is susceptible to varying interpretations, the amounts reported in the consolidated financial statements could change at a 
later date upon final determination by the tax authorities.

33.	 FINANCIAL RISK MANAGEMENT OBJECTIVES AND POLICIES
The Group’s principal financial liabilities comprise loans, trade and other payables. The main purpose of these financial 
liabilities is to finance the Group’s operations. The Group has loan, trade and other receivables, and cash and short-term 
deposits that arise directly from its operations. The Group also hold available-for-sale investments. The Group does not hold 
or issue derivative financial instruments.
The Group is exposed to market risk, credit risk and liquidity risk.
Management reviews and agrees policies for managing each of these risks which are summarised below.
Market risk
Market risk is the risk that the fair value of future cash flows of a financial instrument will fluctuate because of changes in 
market prices. Market prices comprise four types of risk: interest rate risk, currency risk, commodity price risk and other 
price risk, such as equity price risk. Financial instruments affected by market risk include loans, deposits and available-for-
sale investments.
The sensitivity analyses in the following sections relate to the position as at 31 December 2019 and 31 December 2018.
The sensitivity analyses have been prepared on the basis that the amount of net debt, the ratio of fixed to floating interest 
rates of the debt and the proportion of financial instruments in foreign currencies are all constant.
In calculating the sensitivity analyses, management assumed that:
• the statement of the consolidated balance sheet relates to available-for-sale debt instrument; and
• the sensitivity of the relevant consolidated income statement item is the effect of the assumed changes in respective 
market risks. This is based on the financial assets and financial liabilities held at 31 December 2019 and 31 December 2018.
Interest rate risk
Interest rate risk is the risk that the fair value or future cash flows of a financial instrument will fluctuate because of changes 
in market interest rates. The Group’s exposure to market risk for changes in interest rate relates primarily to the Group’s 
cash and short-term deposits and borrowings. These investments are mainly short term in nature and they are not held for 
speculative purposes.
The Group manages interest rate risk by looking at the competitive structure of the market to obtain rates which are 
favourable for its purposes within its risk management limits.
Interest rate sensitivity
A sensitivity analysis is not performed for interest rate risk as the Group’s exposure to the interest-rate risk is minimal at 
the reporting date as the loans from banks are short-term with fixed interest rates.
Foreign currency risk
Foreign currency risk is the risk that the fair value or future cash flows of a financial instrument will fluctuate because of 
changes in foreign exchange rates. The Group’s exposure to the risk of changes in foreign exchange rates relates primarily 
to the Group’s operating activities (when revenue or expense is denominated in a different currency from the Group’s 
accounting currency).
The Group is exposed to foreign currency risk in relation to purchases and sales of goods which are denominated in 
currencies other than its accounting currency as disclosed in Note 2.4. The Group manages its foreign currency exposure by 
considering the prevailing and expected market situation when it plans for future purchases and sales of goods denominated 
in foreign currencies, other than increasing natural-hedged proportion. The Group does not employ any derivative financial 
instruments to hedge its foreign currency exposure.
Equity price risk

values of the investment securities. The Group manages equity price risk by placing a limit on equity investments. The Board 
of Directors reviews and approves all equity investment decisions.

Credit risk
Credit risk is the risk that counterparty will not meet its obligations under a financial instrument or customer contract, 
leading to a financial loss. The Group is exposed to credit risk from its operating activities (primarily for trade receivables) and 
from its financing activities, including deposits with banks, foreign exchange transactions and other financial instruments.
Bank deposits
The Group’s bank balances are mainly maintained with well-known banks in Vietnam. The Group’s maximum exposure to 
credit risk for the components of the balance sheet at each reporting dates are the carrying amounts as illustrated in Notes 
3. The Group evaluates the concentration of credit risk in respect to bank deposit as low.
Trade receivables
Customer credit risk is managed by the Group based on its established policy, procedures and control relating to customer 
credit risk management.
Outstanding customer receivables are regularly monitored. The requirement for impairment is analyzed at each reporting 
date on an individual basis for major clients. The Group seeks to maintain strict control over its outstanding receivables and 
has a credit control department to minimize credit risk. In view of the aforementioned and the fact that the Group’s trade 
receivables relate to a large number of diversified customers, there is no significant concentration of credit risk.
Except for the financial assets for which provision have been made as disclosed in Notes 7 and 8, management evaluate all 
financial assets are neither past due nor impaired as they related to recognized and creditworthy counterparties.
Liquidity risk
The liquidity risk is the risk that the Group will encounter difficulty in meeting financial obligation due to shortage of funds. 
The Group’s exposure to liquidity risk arises primarily from mismatches of maturities of financial assets and liabilities.
The Group monitors its liquidity risk by maintain a level of cash and cash equivalents and bank loans deemed adequate by 
management to finance the Group’s operations and to mitigate the effects of fluctuations in cash flows.

The fair value of the financial assets and liabilities are included at the amount at which the instrument could be exchanged 
in a current transaction between willing parties, other than in a forced or liquidation sale.
The following method and assumption were used to estimate the fair values:
• Cash and short-term deposits, trade receivables, trade payables and other current liabilities approximate their carrying 
amounts largely due to the short-term maturities of these instruments.
• Receivables are evaluated by the Group based on parameters such as interest rates, specific country risk factors, individual 
creditworthiness of the customer and the risk characteristics of the financed project. Based on this evaluation, allowances 
are taken to account for the expected losses of these receivables. As at 31 December 2019, the carrying amounts of such 
receivables, net of allowances, are not materially different from their calculated fair values.
• Fair value of quoted notes and bonds is based on price quotations at the reporting date.
• Fair value of available-for-sale financial assets is derived from quoted market prices in active markets, if available.

A MESSAGE FROM THE CHAIRMAN
Dear valued Shareholders, Customers, and Partners:
In 2018, the global economy experienced bouts of volatility. 
US-China trade tensions, the rising tide of trade protectionism, 
the Brexit negotiation process, and high public debt in many 
countries negatively impacted the upward momentum of the 
world economy.
In this context, Vietnam was one of the world’s bright spots 
with the GDP growth rate hitting a ten-year high of 7.08%, while 
containing inflation below 4% for the third consecutive year. 
The Vietnamese GDP per capita is now two-times what it was 
in 2011. Export turnover in 2018 increased by 13.8% compared 
to 2017, of which the export surplus was USD 7.2 billion, the 
largest ever. Particularly in agriculture, actual attainments 
in 2018 exceeded plans and expectations. The contribution 
of agriculture, forestry, fisheries to GDP increased by 3.76%, 
the highest such increase in the last seven years. The export 
turnover was USD 40.02 billion.
2018 also witnessed the strong development of The PAN Group. 
We had two successful capital raising campaigns. First, we 
completed a VND 1,135 billion bond issuance guaranteed by 
ADB’s Credit Guarantee and Investment Facility (CGIF), a trust 
fund rated AA by Standard and Poor’s. The second was the 
issuance of 13.4 million shares to Japan’s Sojitz Corporation, 
which raised VND 817.4 billion.
We continued to expand through mergers and acquisitions. The 
most significant deal increased PAN’s ownership of Sao Ta 
Foods JSC (FIMEX VN) from 20% to 54%, thereby incorporating 
a large food company into our value chain. We also increased 
our ownership in 584 Nha Trang Seafood JSC to 43% and 
acquired 20% of Vietnam Fumigation JSC. In addition, we have 
completed our planned divestment from PAN Services (20% 
of their remaining capital) to focus entirely on agriculture and 
food.
Despite difficulties, The PAN Group achieved high growth. Total 
assets increased by 58% to VND 9.4 trillion with abundant cash. 
Consolidated net revenue reached VND 7,828 billion, up 92% 
compared to 2017. Profit after tax for the parent company’s 
shareholders hit VND 334 billion, exceeding targets by 14%. 
This was driven by profit growth at member companies such as 
Vinaseed (+9%), Bibica (+12%), and the rapid growth of seafood 
companies such as FIMEX VN (+62%) and Aquatex Bentre 
(+136%).
Not only did The PAN Group expand the scale of its business, 
but thanks to our development strategy, which emphasizes 
environmental protection, corporate social responsibility, 
and international best practices, we also enhanced our 
reputation and received wide-spread support in our local 
and global communities. We focus on the application of 
modern technologies to promote environmentally friendly 
production, reduce electricity consumption, and minimize the 
generation of toxic waste. We also apply internal standards 
and monitoring mechanisms to ensure compliance with 
sustainability measures.
Vietnam’s economy is accelerating again thanks to, among 
other factors, the strong desire of the Government to reform and 
increase the Vietnam’s integration with the rest of the world. 
This environment has brought opportunities for businesses, like 
The PAN Group, who have sustainable development strategies.
To grasp these opportunities, in recent years we have 
strengthened our position in the agriculture and food industry 
through capital mobilization, the acquisition of leading 
companies, and the restructuring of human resources and 
management systems. In 2019, we will work on internally 
developed projects, pursue external mergers and acquisitions, 
and increase our ownership rates in current subsidiaries and 
affiliates. Many projects are scheduled for completion within 
the year, including Bibica’s new confectionery factory in Long 
An, Vinaseed’s rice and seed production plant in Dong Thap, 
and PAN-SALADBOWL’s flower and vegetable breeding center 
in Lam Dong. We will also begin work on new projects such 
as an expansion of FIMEX VN’s shrimp farms, a pangasius 
fingerling project at Aquatex Bentre, a high-tech R&D center 
for Vinaseed, and a Tay Nguyen coffee project in Dak Lak.
Understanding The PAN Group’s internal strengths and 
external opportunities, our management team will continue 
to put forth best effort to make PAN into the leading regional 
corporation in agriculture and food, contributing to the 
development of Vietnam and creating value for shareholders.
On behalf of the Board of Directors, I sincerely thank our 
valued shareholders, customers, and partners for their 
continued trust and support. Thank you, as well, to the staff 
for their dedication to the common dream of The PAN Group.
I wish everyone a successful year. In 2019, let us “go faster 
and further” than ever before!
With sincere thanks,

1. GLOBAL MACRO-ECONOMIC SITUATION
The world entered 2018 with optimistic expectations for global economic growth. The 
optimism could be seen in the forecasts of the some of the most-trusted financial 
institutions in the world, such as the IMF and the World Bank. The factors leading to 
this optimism were the presence of government policies meant to stabilize energy 
and commodity prices, increased confidence in the business environment, and the 
positive effects of Industry 4.0 revolutions.
However, in 2018, the world experienced historic fluctuations that negatively impacted 
the global economy. Most prominently, the trade war between the United States and 
China, and the fierce responses from other countries, has increased global trade 
tension. The worldwide economy has lost a part of the momentum it gained from 
the strong growth of 2017. In addition, the disruption caused by Britain’s upcoming 
departure from the EU and the staggering of the worldwide stock market created the 
difficulties for global economic growth in 2018. Developing economies and emerging 
markets have been heavily affected by the withdrawal of foreign capital and the 
tendency to de-liberalize trade.

Rice industry
The rice industry has developed steadily and maintained good growth due to the 
following factors: favorable weather conditions, deliberate and scientific planting 
operations, and the replacement of traditional rice varieties with high-quality 
varieties following the VietGAP production model.
The current area under rice plantation is estimated at 7.57 million hectares, 
an increase of 134.8 thousand hectares compared to the previous year. The 
productivity of this land is estimated at 58.1 quintal/ha, an increase of 2.6 quintal/
ha, y/y. Although the total area of rice cultivation shrank due to shifts in production 
structure and changes in land use, land productivity increased so that rice 
production grew by 1.24 million tons, to 43.98 million, compared to 2017.
2018 was also an impressive year for Vietnam’s rice export market with more 
than 6.1 million tons of rice exported, bringing an estimated USD 3.03 billion, a 
16.1% increase compared to 2017. White rice made up 50% of total turnover, while 
jasmine and aromatic rice accounted for 32%, glutinous rice for 12% and Japonica 
rice for 5%. 
The value of Vietnam’s rice export turnover has returned to the USD 3 billion mark 
after 6 years of continuous decline, in large part due to the change in planting 
emphasis away from traditional rice varieties towards fragrant and high-quality 
varieties. Vietnamese rice is currently exported to more than 150 countries 
worldwide, including the Americas and various Middle Eastern nations. 
In 2018, the rice industry continued to focus on sustainable production, increasing 
quality and value in the domestic market, and export of high-quality rice varieties, 
with an emphasis on food safety and traceability.

According to the Vietnam Cashew Association (Vinacas) report, the Vietnamese 
cashew sector continued to be the global number one in processing and exporting

In the 2017-2018 season, also according to Vinacas, cashew nut processing and

its current inability to produce sufficient quantities of nuts domestically. As a result, 
Vietnam must import up to 70% of the cashews it processes. This inability to control 
the production of the cashews themselves, combined with a rise in the price of the 
raw nuts, forced many small operators out of business. The cashew sector was also 
hurt by the rising trade tensions between the US and China. These tensions resulted 
in a decline in consumption for these two markets. They, as well as the EU, also 
began to use food quality and food safety regulations as trade barriers by applying 
more stringent standards to foreign suppliers.
 
2019 is expected to be a difficult year for the cashew market.  For many, the strategy

Currently, the world price of shrimp is at historical lows and the United States is

Vietnam’s shrimp industry is still expected to grow in the near term thanks to the EU 
Free Trade Agreement (EVFTA), expected to take effect in 2019. The EU is Vietnam’s 
single largest shrimp export market. The total value of shrimp exported to the EU 
in the first 11 months of 2018 was 779.7 million USD, equivalent to the same period 
last year and accounting for 23.8% of Vietnam’s total shrimp exports. When the 
EVFTA agreement takes effect, it will increase the competitiveness of Vietnamese 
shrimp and shrimp products v. products exported from Thailand, Vietnam’s major 
competitor in this area. Vietnam’s export tax to the EU will drop to 0%, while 
Thailand’s will remain at 20%.

exported to China, the United States, Southeast Asia, the European Union, South

Annually Vietnam plants over 27,000 hectares with a wide variety of ornamental 
flowers, and the planted area is steadily increasing to meet the growing demands 
of domestic and foreign markets. In 2018, hectarage devoted to flower production in 
San Thang, Lai Chau, increased by 60% compared to the same period in 2017. 
According to Trademap statistics, the export value of Vietnam’s fresh cut flowers in 
2017 was USD 37.8 million, up 1.35% from 2016. The compound annual growth rate 
of the period from 2010 - 2017 was 12.1%. Vietnam’s main flower export markets are 
Japan (accounting for 77.9% of export value in 2017), followed by Australia (6.5%) and 
China (6.2%). There was also substantial growth in smaller markets; for example, 
the value of flowers exported to Korea nearly doubled compared to 2017.
 
The flower industry does face some challenges. As with raw cashew nuts, Vietnam 
must import most of its flower seeds. This is inefficient, relative to generating seed 
domestically, and limits the export value of the industry. The problem isn’t confined 
to floriculture. According to statistics from the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural 
Development, about 80-95% of Vietnam’s plant seeds, including flowers, must be 
imported. Producing the desired varieties requires investment and technology that 
Vietnam currently lacks.  
Additionally, the most popular flower varieties desired by export markets are owned 
by non-Vietnamese organizations and the purchase of copyrights will be very costly. 
Moreover, consumer demand for flower varieties is unpredictable and tends to 
change rapidly. Vietnam’s floriculturists need to focus on researching and producing 
new varieties in order to develop special products for Vietnam.

A. BUSINESS SPECIFIC 
RISKS
I. THE AGRICULTURAL SEGMENT
The PAN Group’s agricultural 
business is carried out through 
2 subsidiaries, Vietnam National 
Seed JSC (Vinaseed), PAN-SAL-
ADBOWL JSC, and an affiliate, 
Vietnam Fumigation JSC (VFC). 
The Group faces the normal 
risks of the industry including:
Demand Risk 
Demand risk refers to the possibility of 
lower than expected consumer demand 
for a firm’s products or services. This 
risk is realized whenever Vinaseed, 
VFC, or PAN-SALADBOWL lose access 
to, share within, or fail to penetrate, a 
target market. 
For 
Vinaseed, 
the 
realization 
of 
demand risk comes mostly as a 
consequence of competitive pressure. 
While 
Vinaseed 
is 
an 
important 
seed producer within Vietnam, the 
Vietnamese seed industry as a whole 
is still young and modernizing. Only in 
the last 20 years have farmers started 
to use high-quality and high-yield seed 
varieties, rather than relying on seed 
gathered by traditional, and much less 
capital intensive, methods. The market 
is split between 260 companies. Each 
province has its own seeds, with no 
truly dominant varieties, and the 
product quality is uneven. Domestic 
producers have to compete with 
standardized, 
high-quality 
imports 
sold by larger and more organized 
agribusinesses. All of these factors 
lead to low competitiveness and low 
price – both embodiments of realized 
demand risk. 
For VFC, realization of demand risk 
also tends to result from competition. 
Aside from this, there are reputational 
threats that menace the industry 
generally. Over the past few years, 
the agrochemicals market has been 
scandalized by the sale of fake and/
or counterfeit goods. The scandals 
have created hesitation in the minds of 
potential customers, leading to lower 
revenue.
PAN-SALADBOWL 
faces 
less 
imminent demand risks because its 
joint-venture partner has signed a 
contract to import their entire crop. In 
addition, PAN-SALADBOWL’s flower 
production will likely only meet half of 
the Japanese partner’s demand.
Solutions to minimize risk:
To minimize this risk, Vinaseed has 
conducted many surveys to assess 
market conditions. It has also tried to 
increase the quality of its offerings by 
participating in research and technology 
transfers that allow it to produce seed 
varieties with high yields and strong 
disease resistance characteristics, such 
as RVT and HN88. In addition, Vinaseed 
constantly offers discounts and sends 
officers to give free technology training 
to farmers.
VFC has continuously surveilled the 
market, 
researched 
and 
developed 
flexible sales policies, and attempted to 
optimize costs.
 
Operational Risk: Weather
Operational risk is the possibility that 
a firm will suffer losses greater than 
forecast 
from 
insufficient 
internal 
processes or external events beyond 
its control.  Adverse weather is an 
important operational risk that directly 
threatens the core production activities 
of Vinaseed and PAN-SALADBOWL. 
When such risk is realized, it reduces 
crop yield, crop quality, and tends to 
result in increased seed consumption. 
Vietnam’s 
central 
highlands 
are 
ideal for certain kinds of cultivation; 
however, they are also home to frequent 
damaging rainstorms and periodic 
droughts, both of which have a negative 
impact on agricultural operations.  
Solutions to minimize risk: 
To 
minimize 
operational 
risks, 
especially those posed by adverse 
weather 
events, 
Vinaseed 
has 
expanded, and will continue to expand, 
its production areas into different 
ecological zones. It has also maintained 
warehouses in Dong Van and Ba Vi 
since 2015, where it stockpiles goods to 
ensure continuity of production in case 
of supply disruption. Finally, Vinaseed 
is researching and developing products 
with cold, drought, pest and disease 
resistance properties to reduce the 
impact of natural disasters and climate 
change on crop yields.
PAN-SALADBOWL conducts most of 
its planting and growing operations 
in Belgian and Dutch greenhouses, 
complemented by Israeli irrigation 
and dike systems. This makes their 
operations less likely to be affected by 
adverse weather.
Supply Risk: Risks to Agricultural 
Land Viability  
Supply risk is the possibility that a 
firm will be unable to source the raw 
materials it requires for its basic 
activities. The most fundamental and 
troubling source of supply risk in 
Vietnam’s agricultural sector is the 
increasing scarcity and fragmentation 
of land. We cannot grow crops if we 
do not have adequate amounts or 
concentrations of land on which to grow 
them. Vietnam’s agricultural land is 
highly fragmented due to the nature 
of the terrain, high population density, 
land allocations, culture, and history. 
The area available for cultivation 
shrinks gradually every year due to 
urbanization and industrialization. The 
reduction of available hectarage has 
had consequences for all Vietnamese 
agriculture, but especially for rice 
production.
There are, however, bright spots. 
The central highlands, including Lam 
Dong province, have very favorable 
conditions 
for 
planting. 
PAN-
SALADBOWL’s 
operations 
benefit 
from these favorable conditions and it 
is buying more land in the area. 
 Solutions to minimize risk:
To minimize further realization of this 
risk, the company has cooperated with 
local authorities to actively restructure 
planting areas and promote the use of 
high-quality plant varieties meant to 
improve farmers’ income, help farmers 
sell their crop, keep them on the land, 
and prevent further reductions in the 
area under cultivation.

Labor Demand Fluctuations
The PAN Group’s demand for labor fluctuates with 
market demand. The availability of labor is inelastic 
relative to consumer demand, and corporate 
attempts to compensate incur opportunity costs 
or negative effects on production and product 
quality. Conversely, when market demand is low or 
conditions unfavorable, The PAN Group experiences 
a reduced need for labor. It is not possible to maintain 
wage levels under adverse market conditions and so 
wages may need to be cut. Mass layoffs may also 
occur. Such disruptions are bad for Group’s image. 
Maintaining employment stability and continuous 
growth is a challenge. 
Solutions to minimize risk: 
The PAN Group minimizes the various risks created 
by fluctuations in labor demand by developing 
appropriate human resource policies, following 
labor 
regulations, 
participating 
in 
collective 
labor agreements. All member companies have 
trade unions, have signed collective bargaining 
agreements, and have dialogue mechanisms by 
which workers may attempt to resolve grievances.
Occupational Health and Safety Issues
Occupational illness and injury are serious concerns 
for all businesses. However, this risk is especially acute 
for certain categories of worker: those exposed to 
potentially dangerous materials, weather conditions, 
or who work with heavy machinery. Maintaining 
a strong safety record is important for each PAN 
employee but is also important for maintaining the 
Group’s ability to attract competent workers and 
defend brand reputation.
Solutions to minimize risk: 
The PAN Group addresses health and safety 
concerns by ensuring the availability of safety 
equipment in its facilities and by implementing 
a thorough inspection regime. For positions or 
facilities associated with more significant risks, 
specific safety training is provided, as for forklift, 
boiler operation, welding and toxic chemical use. 
The PAN Group tests the swimming ability of all 
personnel frequently exposed to large bodies of 
water.
Responsibility to Customers
The homes and bodies of our customers 
are the final destinations for The PAN 
Group’s products. For this reason, the 
safety and quality of these products 
must be taken seriously. It is the 
producer’s responsibility to provide 
customers with affordable, high-quality 
products, as well as reasonable post-
purchase services. If we fail at this, we 
risk incurring reductions in our market 
share, damage to our brand, and the 
ultimate loss of the customer.
Solutions to minimize risk: 
The PAN Group has invested heavily 
in ensuring food safety and improving 
product quality. All food factories 
currently meet international standards 
such as HACCP, BRC, FSSC22000. 
All agricultural products comply with 
safe 
production 
standards 
under 
various certifications such as VietGAP, 
GLOBALG.A.P., and ASC. Relevant 
information about products is provided 
so that customers can evaluate their 
suitability. Customers can also always 
contact the company. 
Human Rights
Operational risks arise from workplace 
abuse,

II. Commodity price risks
The PAN Group and its subsidiaries operate in many different fields that are sensitive to the price 
of commodities: agriculture, seafoods. Adverse commodity price fluctuations are a realization of 
supply risk when member companies require these commodities as inputs. They are realizations 
of demand risk whenever a member needs to sell materials it produces to a third party. Rapid 
changes in commodity prices can damage The PAN Group’s business and operations. 
Solutions to minimize risk
The PAN Group manages commodity price risks through carefully monitoring domestic and foreign 
markets, ensuring timely commodity purchases, production planning, and prudent stockpiling. 
Risks related to commodity price fluctuations are monitored by the purchasing department, the 
production departments of subsidiaries, and reported to Director of Production and Chief Executive 
Officer on a weekly basis.
III. Interest Rate Risks
The PAN Group’s interest rate risk exposure mainly comes from short-term liabilities as well as 
short-term deposits of the company and some of its subsidiaries. 
Solutions to minimize risk
The PAN Group  manages interest rate risks by carefully monitoring relevant markets, including 
currency markets. The PAN Group’s Accounting-Finance Department and those of member 
companies produce forecasts, sensitivity  analyses, and adjust leverage and investment strategies 
according to their prevailing view of interest rate risk.   
In 2018, The PAN Group mostly used equity and cash from fixed-rate bond to carry out investment 
activities. Therefore, it is not significantly exposed to interest rate movements. Additionally, 
many member company’s can access favorable loans with low or fixed-interest rates from 
banks reducing their exposure to interest rate changes. The PAN Group deposits are also held at 
institutions willing to provide the greatest benefits to the Group and the shareholders.   
Interest risk is monitored by the Finance-Accounting Departments at member companies, the 
Finance-Accounting Department of the Group.
IV. Exchange rate risk
Exchange rate risk is the risk of loss 
due to adverse changes in exchange 
rates and it arises whenever The 
PAN Group or affiliates engage 
in 
transactions 
denominated 
in 
currencies other than the Vietnamese 
Dong. The PAN Group is exposed to 
this risk through its subsidiaries 
and affiliates engaged in import 
and export and whenever they raise 
foreign capital. 
Solutions to minimize risks
The PAN Group estimates exchange 
rate risk through the issuance of 
shares for capital increase and has 
adjustment policies for incomes with 
foreign currency elements, export 
mechanisms, 
and 
trade 
credit. 
Import and export plans are carefully 
developed to limit exchange rate risk. 
Of The PAN Group’s subsidiaries, 
Aquatex Bentre, FIMEX VN, VFC, Pan-
SALADBOWL and Lafooco have the 
largest FX risk exposure. As Aquatex 
Bentre and FIMEX VN buy raw materials 
within Vietnam and export their finished 
products, they benefit from the relative 
depreciation of the Dong. The import 
and export operations of Lafooco and 
VFC are controlled and monitored 
more closely, since they source most of 
their inputs abroad. Companies seek to 
minimize the impact of exchange rate 
fluctuations generally.
E. Risks Arising from Mergers and 
Acquisitions
Aside from normal economic risks, 
the acquisition and integration of 
another company into the Group can 
create cultural clashes and changes of 
personnel that are disruptive of desired 
group synergies.
Solutions to minimize risk:

always

defines M&A strategies; reasonably

from a proper M&A strategy. PAN has

as effectively handled issues after

combination between the subsidiaries. 
The management of operations and 
human resource in the post-acquistion 
period areis always taken care of in 
order to maximize the potential value 
of the subsidiaries and the M&A deal.
In 2018 and the previous years, PAN 
has not had significant changes in key 
personnel, integration of corporate 
culture, or the ability to create 
synergies in post-investment period.

Operational risk is the risk of loss due 
to inadequate internal processes or 
due to the impacts of external events. 
There are many kinds of operational 
risks, including compliance risks, IT 
security risks, and human resource 
management risks.

Compliance risk is operational risk 
arising from the potential damage done 
to The PAN Group due to employee or 
member non-compliance with laws, 
regulations, rules, and standards.
Solutions to minimize risk
The 
Risk

of

• Ensure employees in charge of

violators 
of 
internal 
company standards.

The PAN Group is exposed to legal 
risk from disputes that arise during 
the course of business with its 
counterparties and from a shifting 
regulatory 
environment. 
Legal 
documents and related guidelines are

Solutions to minimize risk:

a Department of Law and Compliance.

directly to The PAN Group’s Board 
of Directors. They study the likely 
effects of new regulations from the

Credit 
risk 
directly 
affects 
the 
business operations (mainly customer 
receivables) and financial operations 
of The PAN Group, including its 
bank 
deposits, 
foreign 
exchange 
transactions, 
and 
other 
financial 
instruments. 
Solutions to minimize risk
To effectively control credit risk, The 
PAN Group periodically considers the 
creditworthiness of customers and 
the condition of its deposits and other 
financial instruments. The Group has 
focused on maintaining strict control 
over outstanding customer receivables 
and employs credit control staff to 
reduce risk. The PAN Group approves 
a list of customers based on their 
financial situation and payment history 
on a quarterly and yearly basis. 
The credit risk of deposit balances is 
managed by the treasurer. Only large, 
high-profile banks shall be chosen 
for deposit placement. We maintain a 
system of continuous risk reporting to 
closely monitor these operations.
I. Liquidity risk
Liquidity risk occurs when The PAN 
Group 
faces 
difficulties 
fulfilling 
financial obligations due to cash 
shortages. For The PAN Group, this 
risk arises when the maturity dates of 
financial assets and financial liabilities 
are mismatched. 
Solutions to minimize risk
The PAN Group tightly manages its 
cash flow and maintains a reasonable 
amount of cash and deposits. It also 
arranges short-term and long-term 
credit 
contracts 
with 
banks 
and 
other financial institutions to ensure 
loans will be repaid after the Group 
completes financial plans, maintains 
liquidity indexes at healthy levels, and 
maintains a balanced ratio between 
assets and liabilities. Every month, cash 
flow and liquidity position statements 
are made by the relevant departments 
and reported to the Executive Board. 
The PAN Group faces low liquidity risk.
K. Other risks: Systematic and Non-
Systematic Risks
In 
addition 
to 
the 
risk 
factors 
mentioned above, The PAN Group is 
aware of systematic risk factors, such 
as fire, natural disasters, war, and 
large-scale disease epidemics. The 
realization of these risks is unusual, 
but would be catastrophic, with the 
potential to cause long-term damage 
to the well-being of The PAN Group. 
Solutions to minimize risk: 
Systematic risk cannot be diversified 
away, it can only be insured against. 
The PAN Group has assessed the risk 
in each field of its operations and the 
damage level that would occur from 
each. Where appropriate it has insured 
itself against systematic risk. 
In 2018, The PAN Group bought 
systematic 
and 
unsystematic 
risk 
insurance for member companies 
in the agriculture and the fisheries 
sectors whose business activities are 
more likely to be disturbed by weather 
and disease.

2.1. M&A at The PAN Group
M&A at Vietnam Fumigation Company (VFC)
Rationale
Vietnam Fumigation Company is a leader in the field of agricultural materials production and trading. It represents 
an important component of the agricultural production value chain that the PAN Group is assembling. VFC shows 
outstanding potential. It shows this potential now, more than ever by cooperating with PAN to augment their already-
impressive resources and experience. 
• Agrochemical:  VFC has more than 25 years of experience in Vietnam’s agrochemical space and accounts for 7% of 
market share. VFC is the second largest in the industry with revenue of VND 1,900 billion and a nationwide distribution 
system. VFC is also a long-time distributor for many large global agro-pharmaceutical companies (e.g. Syngenta, 
Kumiai, Nippon...). 
• Fumigation (for agricultural export): VFC has more than 30 years of experience in fumigation and accounts for 60% of 
market share. Annual revenue is about VND 300 billion (accounting for 11% of total revenue but contributing to 22% of PBT). 
VFC joined the International Maritime Disinfection Organization (IMFO) in 1999 and obtained ISO 9001: 2000 BVQI-UKAS / 
ANSI-RAB certificate in 2001.
• VFC has a nationwide distribution network with 16 branches and more than 2,500 level-2 certified agrochemical agents as 
well as 2,300 customers / fumigation agents.
• Long-standing brand: VFC is a professional and reputable company in the field of agrochemicals, disinfection, and pest 
control. Customers who export agricultural products to tightly regulated markets, such as in the EU, Japan, and United 
States, prioritize VFC over other companies.
• VFC has an experienced management team who are committed to the long -term growth of the company. Their company 
culture and values  serve to promote the development of strong  relationships within their network of agents and customers. 
Experience, long-term commitment, and social capital are key factors in the successful unfolding of what will become a 
fruitful relationship between VFC and the PAN Group.
Method & 
Progress
From the end of 2018 to the beginning of 2019, the PAN Group increased its ownership in VFC, as follows:
• November, 2018: The PAN Group bought 6,323,000 shares in VFC, equivalent to 20% of the charter capital of VFC with 
a total investment value of VND 243 billion. Capital source: the PAN Group’s own capital.  
• December, 2018: The PAN Group officially and publicly acquired  an additional 6,916,061 shares in VFC, raising PAN’s 
ownership to 41.88% of VFC’s chartered capital with a total investment value of VND 510 billion. Capital source: the PAN 
Group’s own capital. 
Investment 
result
• On December 31, 2018, the PAN Group owned 20% of VFC’s charter capital. PAN began a public bid to increase its own-
ership during an implementation period between December 3, 2018 and January 3, 2019.  The PAN Group officially held 
41.88% of VFC’s chartered capital from 9/1/2019.  
• It is expected that in 2019, The PAN Group will continue to increase its ownership in VFC. VFC continues to achieve positive 
growth and represents an important contribution to the PAN Group’s consolidated profit.

in Japan. With these advantages, Aquatex Ben Tre is highly appreciated and actively supported by the PAN Group.

trading and has shifted its focus to high value-added products.

2018 Performance: 2018 was marked by impressive growth at Fimex VN. Revenue reached VND 4,884 billion, exceeding the 
2018 target by 12%. Consumption volume increased 10% from the previous year. Fimex VN’s profits before tax reached VND 211 
billion, 51% in excess of the target. This is also the greatest year-on-year surge in profit that Fimex VN has seen in its history. This 
momentum comes from rising demand in large import markets, such as the EU and the US, in the context of increasing tensions 
related to global trade..
Fimex VN’s products are high value-added products and the company has been successful retaining long-term customers 
who have come to expect high quality and stable prices. Fimex VN has taken proactive measures to control sources for clean 
shrimp material, implement traceability, and export to difficult markets such as Japan, America, and Europe. The company’s 
executive has considerable experience in making timely market forecasts. Fimex VN has prepared for contingencies by arranging 
to purchase raw materials from outside sources and maintain stable, maximum-capacity production. The company’s successful 
off-season shrimp farming effort in 2017 also brought excellent profits in the first months of 2018.
Profit Margin: In 2018, Fimex VN achieved a net profit margin of 5% and gross profit margin of 10%, the highest rates in the last 
5 years.

. In addition to its M&A and cooperation with strategic partners, The PAN Group continues to 
implement its sustainable development strategy and connect member companies. The consensus 
and support of member companies at each step is necessary for The PAN Group to implement a long-
term socio-environmental strategy.
Evaluation of The Board 
of Directors on Socio-environmental 
Responsibility
Environmentally and socially responsible production practices 
are enforced according to international standards; these include 
the IFC’s performance standards and the ADB’s Safeguard 
Policy Statement. PAN’s 2018 Annual Socio-Environmental 
Assessment indicates the strong cooperation of member 
company management with respect to both general strategy and 
specific implementation.
ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION IN PRODUCTION: 
MATERIALS, ENERGY, WATER, WASTE…
Plastic waste is a global problem and food packaging is a 
significant source of such waste. Therefore, companies in the 
Group have gradually begun to use self-degrading packaging, 
packaging from natural materials such as jute, hemp or non-
woven fabric, etc. The shift reflects a practical approach to the 
problem and shows our commitment to develop business in 
association with environmental protection responsibility.
Companies are naturally interested in energy savings, if only 
for economic reasons, particularly in industries that require 
freezing and refrigeration, such as seafood processing. Energy 
usage at all member companies is monitored and analyzed, and 
the results are used to reduce the energy consumed per unit of 
product, ensuring that the production process meets economic 
and environmental objectives.
The protection of water resources in agriculture and fishery 
industries are essential to product quality, productivity, and 
environmental preservation. Member companies strictly adhere 
to international standards in water and agricultural 
sustainability, such as GLOBALG.A.P., ASC, and 
BAP. They strive to improve production processes 
and continually implement new technologies in the 
interest of protecting water resources. 
Industrial waste is another key environmental 
concern. Wherever possible, companies aim to 
repurpose recyclable waste as fuel or compost, and 
waste water is treated and recirculated. Hazardous 
waste is collected and processed in strict accordance 
with environmental and health regulations.

REPLACEMENT OF THE TOP MANAGER AND APPOINTMENT OF NEW MEMBERS OF 
SUB-COMMITTEES UNDER THE BOARD OF DIRECTORS
In May 2018, the Group welcomed the Vice-Chairwoman of the Board of Directors, 
Ms. Nguyen Thi Tra My, to her new position as Chief Executive Officer of The PAN 
Group.  
Ms. Nguyen’s leadership and vision for the Group will complement existing plans to 
raise capital and meet the demand for rapid, sustainable development. 
Additionally, following corporate governance best practices, new members of the 
sub-committees were appointed to ensure that independent members comprise at 
least 1/3 of total committee members. In certain committees, 2/3 of the members 
are independent. 
ADDING MEMBER COMPANIES AND INCREASING OWNERSHIP IN SUBSIDIARIES
The PAN Group welcomed an important new affiliate in November 2018. Vietnam 
Fumigation Company (VFC) has accumulated more than 20 years of experience in 
agrochemical production and distribution. Affiliation with VFC represents a major 
step forward in the Group’s long-term strategy to develop an integrated value chain. 
The aim of this strategy is to transform The PAN Group into a regional leader in 
agriculture and food.  
Consistent with the Group’s commitment to developing its core business, the Group 
also increased its ownership of Vinaseed and Aquatex Bentre.
REFORMS TO INCREASE TRANSPARENCY, COMPLIANCE, AND PERFORMANCE 
STANDARDS IN MANAGEMENT
Corresponding with increased capital and organizational improvement in 2018, The 
PAN Group reviewed and improved key regulations, procedures, and guidelines. 
- The PAN Group issued a new version of the Charter. The new charter reflects 
updates to the business model, scale, and performance of the Group.
- The PAN Group developed and issued “Internal Regulations for the Corporate 
Governance of The PAN Group.” These regulations were developed with reference to 
corporate governance best practices and based on consideration of corporate governance 
requirements in Vietnam. The regulations enact key measures to protect the rights and 
interests of shareholders and enforce standards for behavior and business ethics for 
members of BOD, BOS, Management Team and other managers at The PAN Group.
- The PAN Group completed and registered internal labor regulations to safeguard 
the legitimate rights and interests of the Group’s employees.
STAFF IN CHARGE OF CORPORATE GOVERNANCE
In compliance with Decree 71/2017/NĐ-CP, “Guidelines for the Corporate Governance 
of Listed Companies,” the Group appointed an individual to monitor and enforce 
corporate governance. This individual is responsible for ensuring compliance with 
procedures related to General Meetings of Shareholders and BOD/BOS meetings, 
resolutions issuing therefrom, and disclosing required information, etc.

GENERAL INFORMATION OF THE PAN GROUP
The PAN Group Overview
In 2018, The PAN Group has continued to build a 
solid foundation in agriculture and food through 
mergers and acquisitions of new companies with 
good fundamentals, high growth potential, wide 
distribution systems, and by increased investment 
in existing affiliates and subsidiaries.  At the same 
time, to support rapid development, The PAN Group 
has also successfully mobilized large amounts of 
capital from international organizations. The PAN 
Group has worked to improve the capacity, financial 
management, and growth strategies of its member 
companies, all in service of the ultimate objective: 
to become a regional pioneer in agriculture and 
food, providing high-quality, traceable products to 
domestic and international markets.
By the end of 2018, Vietnam’s economy 
had witnessed the highest GDP growth 
rate in the past 10 years, at 7.08%, while 
the agricultural sector grew 2.89%, the 
highest such rate since 2012, continuing 
its recovery from previous lows.  In that 
context, The PAN Group maintained an 
impressive growth rate relative to 2017 
within its two core areas of operation, 
agriculture and food.

Farm) and food (PAN Food) segments 
contributed VND 4.448 trillion (56.8%) 
and 
VND 
2.404 
trillion 
(30.7%) 
respectively. The remaining VND 976 
billion (12%) was post-consolidation 
Q4 revenue from FIMEX VN.
The PAN Groups growth is due to the 
successes of member companies and 
its M&A strategy.
• Profit: Consolidated profit was VND 
637 billion before tax and VND 567 
billion after tax, up 17% and 13%, 
respectively, from 2017. Profit to PAN 
shareholders reached VND 334 billion, 
exceeding expectations by 14%.
The PAN Group’s positive profit 
growth can be attributed to strong 
yearly profits at a number of member 
companies, like Vinaseed (VND 252 
billion, up 9%), and Bibica (VND 
110 billion, up 13%), as well as 
extraordinary seafood industry returns 
from FIMEX VN (VND 177 billion, up 
56%) and Aquatex Bentre (VND 67 
billion, up 139%).
Thanks to its mergers, acquisitions, 
and the growth of member companies, 
The PAN Group’s 2018 assets totaled 
VND 9.439 trillion, an increase of VND 
3.466 trillion, equivalent to 158% of

remained reasonably balanced, with 
total liabilities at VND 3.465 trillion 
(37% of total assets), of which short-
term debt comprised VND 1.778 
trillion, and long-term debt VND

2. SUBCOMMITTEES OF THE BOARD OF DIRECTORS
On July 15, 2013, the Board of Directors issued Resolution No. 16-07 / 2013 / NQ-HĐQT to 
establish four subcommittees to support the Board’s activities: The Investment Subcommittee, 
the Human Resources Subcommittee, the Social Responsibility Subcommittee, and the 
Independent Management Subcommittee. The Investment Subcommittee was obviated by 
establishment of the Investment Council at the 2014 Annual General Meeting of Shareholders, 
as stipulated in Clause 3, Article 29 of the Charter of the PAN Pacific Joint Stock Company, 
issued on October 28, 2014. Accordingly, Resolution No. 15-06 / 2014 / NQ-HĐQT dismissed the 
Investment Subcommittee and cancelled all pertinent documents.
On April 6, 2015, the Board established the Subcommittee for the Environment and 
Sustainable Development to promote the Company’s sustainable development activities. 
This subcommittee reflects the Company’s commitment to professionalizing its supervision 
of its social and environmental impacts, good corporate citizenship, and regulating its future 
expansion according to sustainability protocols. Members who contribute to the committee 
possess a comprehensive understanding of the Company’s activities, are experienced in social, 
environmental, and safety issues, and have received international training in these areas at 
corporations such as Sumitomo, Yamaha, CJ Vina, Palffiger, and Levi Strauss. The Environment 
and Sustainable Development Subcommittee was established under Resolution No. 04-04 / 
2015 / NQ-HĐQT on April 6, 2015.
The AGM subsequently approved cancellation of the Investment Council and its regulatory 
provisions. The rights and obligations of the Investment Council were transferred in accordance 
with the current Charter for the Board, under Resolution No. 01-04 / 2015 / NQ-DHDCD, Article 
7, Clause B, issued on April 24, 2015.
 
On November 18, 2018, the Board of Directors issued a resolution to restructure their 
subcommittees according to the corporate governance provisions of Decree 71/2017 / ND-CP 
and Internal Regulations adopted by the General Meeting of Shareholders on October 27, 2018. 
The Board of Directors approved renaming the Environment and Sustainable Development 
Subcommittee as the Sustainable Development Subcommittee.
As of December 31, 2018, the Company has three subcommittees under the Board, including the 
Personnel Subcommittee, the Sustainable Development Subcommittee, and the Independent 
Subcommittee.
