The cost of an intangible asset comprises its purchase price and any directly attributable costs of preparing the intangible 
asset for its intended use.
Expenditures for additions, improvements are added to the carrying amount of the assets and other expenditures are charged 
to the consolidated income statement as incurred.
When intangible assets are sold or retired, any gain or loss resulting from their disposal (the difference between the net 
disposal proceeds and the carrying amount) is included in the consolidated income statement.
Land use rights (“LURs”)
LURs are recorded as intangible assets if the land is held for use in the production and business or for rent to others by the Group 
and when the Group receives the LUR certificate. The cost of LUR comprises any directly attributable costs of preparing the land for 
its intended use. Land with indefinite useful file is not amortised.
The advance payment for land rental, of which the land lease contracts have effectiveness prior to 2003 and land use right 
certificate being issued, are recorded as intangible asset according to Circular No. 45/2013/TT-BTC issued by the Ministry of 
Finance on 25 April 2013 providing guideline for the management, use and calculation of depreciation or amortisation of assets 
(“Circular 45”).
Copyrights
Copyrights of maize and rice varieties are recognized at the purchase price for varieties not researched and developed by the 
Company and its subsidiaries. Copyrights are amortized on a straight-line basis over the short period of time between the 
estimated useful life and the time of purchase.

3.7 BORROWING COSTS
Borrowing costs consist of interest and other costs that the Group incurs in connection with the borrowing of funds and are 
recorded as expense during the period in which they are incurred, except to the extent that they are capitalized as explained 
in the following paragraph.
Borrowing costs that are directly attributable to the acquisition, construction or production of an asset that necessarily take 
a substantial period of time to get ready for its intended use or sale are capitalized as part of the cost of the respective asset
3.8 INVESTMENT PROPERTIES
Investment properties are stated at cost including transaction costs less accumulated depreciation. Investment properties 
held for capital appreciation are not amortised but subject to impairment review.
Subsequent expenditure relating to an investment property that has already been recognized is added to the net book value 
of the investment property when it is probable that future economic benefits, in excess of the originally assessed standard of 
performance of the existing investment property.
Depreciation of investment properties are calculated on a straight-line basis over the estimated useful life of each asset as 
follows:
Buildings and structures
5 - 20 years
Others
6 - 15 years
Investment properties are derecognised when either they have been disposed of or when the investment properties are 
permanently withdrawn from use and no future economic benefit is expected from its disposal. The difference between the 
net disposal proceeds and the carrying amount of the assets is recognised in the consolidated income statement in the year 
of retirement or disposal.
Transfers are made to investment properties when, and only when, there is a change in use, evidenced by ending of owner- 
occupation, commencement of an operating lease to another party or ending of construction or development. Transfers 
are made from investment properties when, and only when, there is change in use, evidenced by commencement of owner- 
occupation or commencement of development with a view to sale. The transfer from investment property to owner-occupied 
property or inventories does not change the cost or the carrying value of the property for subsequent accounting at the date 
of change in use.
3.9  LEASED ASSETS
The determination of whether an arrangement is, or contains a lease is based on the substance of the arrangement at inception 
date and requires an assessment of whether the fulfilment of the arrangement is dependent on the use of specific assets and 
the arrangement conveys a right to use the asset.
Leases are classified as finance leases whenever the terms of the lease transfer substantially all the risks and rewards of 
ownership of the asset to the lessee. All other leases are classified as operating leases.
Where the Group is the lessee
Rentals under operating leases are charged to the consolidated income statement on a straight-line basis over the lease term.
Where the Group is the lessor
Assets subject to operating leases are included as the Group’s investment property in the consolidated balance sheet. Initial 
direct costs incurred in negotiating an operating lease are recognised in the consolidated income statement as incurred.
Lease income is recognised in the consolidated income statement on a straight-line basis over the lease term.

3.10 PREPAID EXPENSES
Prepaid expenses are reported as short-term or long-term prepaid expenses on the consolidated balance sheet and amortised 
over the period for which the amounts are paid or the period in which economic benefit are generated in relation to these 
expenses.
Prepaid for land rental
The prepaid land rental represents the unamortised balance of advance payment made in accordance with lease contracts 
signed after 2003. Such prepaid rental is classified as long-term prepaid expenses for allocation to the consolidated income 
statement over the remaining lease period, according to Circular 45.
Fishery and fishery-related cost
Fishery and fishery-related cost include cost of renting ponds, digging ponds, replenishing ponds, and raising fish. The digging 
ponds, replenishing ponds, and raising fish costs are amortised over the year, in which economic benefits are generated in 
connection to the costs incurred.
3.11 BUSINESS COMBINATIONS AND GOODWILL
Business combinations are accounted for using the purchase method. The cost of a business combination is measured as 
the fair value of assets given, equity instruments issued and liabilities incurred or assumed at the date of exchange plus any 
costs directly attributable to the business combination. Identifiable assets and liabilities and contingent liabilities assumed in 
a business combination are measured initially at fair values at the date of business combination.
Goodwill is initially measured at cost being the excess of the cost of the business combination over the Group’s share in the net 
fair value of the acquiree’s identifiable assets, liabilities and contingent liabilities. If the cost of acquisition is less than the fair 
value of the net assets of the subsidiary acquired, the difference is recognized directly in the consolidated income statement. 
After initial recognition, goodwill is measured at cost less accumulated amortization. Amortization of goodwill is calculated 
on a straight-line basis over ten (10) years during which the source embodying economic benefits are recovered by the Group. 
The parent company conducts the periodical review for impairment of goodwill of investment in subsidiaries. If there are 
indicators of impairment loss incurred is higher than the yearly allocated amount of goodwill on the straight-line basis, the 
higher amount will be recorded in the consolidated income statement.
3.12 INVESTMENTS
Investments in associates
The Group’s investment in its associates is accounted for using the equity method of accounting. An associate is an entity in 
which the Group has significant influence that is neither subsidiaries nor joint ventures. The Group generally deems they have 
significant influence if they have over 20% of the voting rights.
Under the equity method, the investment is carried in the consolidated balance sheet at cost plus post acquisition changes 
in the group’s share of net assets of the associates. Goodwill arising on acquisition of the associate is included in the 
carrying amount of the investment. Goodwill is not amortised and subject to annual review of impairment. The consolidated 
income statement reflects the share of the post-acquisition results of operation of the associates.
The share of post-acquisition profit (loss) of the associates is presented on face of the consolidated income statement and its 
share of post-acquisition movements in reserves is recognised in reserves. The cumulative post-acquisition movements are 
adjusted against the carrying amount of the investment. Dividend receivable from associates reduces the carrying amount of 
the investment.
The financial statements of the associates are prepared for the same reporting year and use the same accounting policies as 
the Group. Where necessary, adjustments are made to bring the accounting policies in line with those of the Group.
Held-for-trading securities and investments in other entities
Held-for-trading securities and investments in other entities are stated at their acquisition costs.
Provision for diminution in value of investments
Provision of the investment is made when there are reliable evidences of the diminution in value of those investments at the 
balance sheet date.
Increases or decreases to the provision balance are recorded as finance expenses in the consolidated income statement.
Held-to-maturity investments
Held-to-maturity investments are stated at their acquisition costs. After initial recognition, held-to-maturity investments 
are measured at recoverable amount. Any impairment loss incurred is recognised as finance expense in the consolidated 
income statement and deducted against the value of such investments.
3.13 PAYABLE AND ACCRUALS
Payable and accrual are recognised for amount to be paid in the future for goods and services received, whether or not billed 
to the Group.
3.14 ACCRUAL FOR SEVERANCE PAY
The severance pay to employee is accrued at the end of each reporting year for all employees who have been in service for 
more than 12 months up to 31 December 2008 at the rate of one-half of the average monthly salary for each year of service up 
to 31 December 2008 in accordance with the Labor Code and related implementing guidance. The average monthly salary used 
in this calculation will be revised at the end of each reporting year following the average monthly salary of the 6-month period 
up to the reporting date.  Increases or decreases to the accrued amount other than actual payment to employee will be taken 
to the consolidated income statement.
This accrued severance pay is used to settle the termination allowance to be paid to employee upon termination of their labour 
contract following Article 48 of the Labor Code.
3.15 FOREIGN CURRENCY TRANSACTIONS
Transactions in currencies other than the Group’s reporting currency of VND are recorded at the actual transaction exchange 
rates at transaction dates which are determined as follows:
•	 Transaction resulting in receivables are recorded at the buying exchange rates of the commercial banks designated for 
collection; and
•	 Transactions resulting in liabilities are recorded at the selling exchange rates of the transaction of commercial banks 
designated for payment.
At the end of the year, monetary balances denominated in foreign currencies are translated at the actual transaction exchange 
rates at consolidated the balance sheet dates which are determined as follows:
•	 Monetary assets are translated at buying exchange rate of the commercial bank where the Group conducts transactions 
regularly; and
•	 Monetary liabilities are translated at selling exchange rate of the commercial bank where the Group conducts transactions 
regularly.
All foreign exchange differences incurred during the year and arising from the revaluation of monetary accounts denominated 
in foreign currency at year-end are taken to the consolidated income statement.

3.16 APPROPRIATION OF NET PROFIT
Net profit after tax (excluding negative goodwill arising from a bargain purchase) is available for appropriation to investors 
after approval by appropriate level of authority, and after making appropriation to reserve funds in accordance with the Group’s 
Charter and Vietnamese regulatory requirements.
The Group maintains the following reserve funds which are appropriated from the Group’s net profit as proposed by the Board 
of Directors and subject to approval by shareholders at the Annual General Meeting.
Investment and development fund
This fund is set aside for use in the Group’s expansion of its operation or of in-depth investments.
Bonus and welfare fund
This fund is set aside for the purpose of pecuniary rewarding and encouraging, common benefits and improvement of the 
employees’ benefits, and presented as a liability on the consolidated balance sheet.
3.17 TREASURY SHARES
Group’s own equity instruments which are reacquired (treasury shares) are recognised at cost and deducted from equity. 
No gain or loss is recognised in profit or loss upon purchase, sale, issue or cancellation of the Group’s own equity instruments.
3.18 EARNINGS PER SHARE
Basic earnings per share amounts are calculated by dividing net profit after tax for the year attributable to ordinary shareholders 
of the Group (after adjusting for the bonus and welfare fund) by the weighted average number of ordinary shares outstanding 
during the year.
Diluted earnings per share amounts are calculated by dividing the net profit after tax attributable to ordinary equity holders of 
the Group by the weighted average number of ordinary shares outstanding during the year plus the weighted average number 
of ordinary shares that would be issued on conversion of all the dilutive potential ordinary shares into ordinary shares.
3.19 REVENUE RECOGNITION
Revenue is recognised to the extent that it is probable that the economic benefits will flow to the Group and the revenue can be 
reliably measured. Revenue is measured at the fair value of the consideration received or receivable, excluding trade discount, 
rebate and sales return. The following specific recognition criteria must also be met before revenue is recognised:
Sale of goods
Revenue is recognised when the significant risks and rewards of ownership of the goods have passed to the buyer, usually 
upon the delivery of the goods.
Rendering of services
Revenue is recognised when the services have been rendered and completed.
Interest
Revenue is recognised as the interest accrues (taking into account the effective yield on the asset) unless collectability is in 
doubt.
Dividends
Income is recognised when the Group’s entitlement as an investor to receive the dividend is established.
3.20 TAXATION
Current income tax
Current income tax assets and liabilities for the current and prior years are measured at the amount expected to be recovered 
from or paid to the taxation authorities. The tax rates and tax laws used to compute the amount are those that are enacted as 
at the balance sheet date.
Current income tax is charged or credited to the consolidated income statement, except when it relates to items recognised 
directly to equity, in which case the current income tax is also dealt with in equity.
Current income tax assets and liabilities are offset when there is a legally enforceable right for the Group to offset current tax 
assets against current tax liabilities and when the Group intends to settle its current tax assets and liabilities on a net basis.
Deferred tax
Deferred tax is provided using the liability method on temporary differences at the balance sheet date between the tax base of 
assets and liabilities and their carrying amount for financial reporting purposes.
Deferred tax liabilities are recognised for all taxable temporary differences, except:
•	 Where the deferred tax liability arises from the initial recognition of an asset or liability in a transaction which at the time of 
the related transaction affects neither the accounting profit nor taxable profit or loss; and
•	 In respect of taxable temporarily differences associated with investments in subsidiaries and associates where timing of 
the reversal of the temporary difference can be controlled and it is probable that the temporary difference will not reverse 
in the foreseeable future.
Deferred tax assets are recognised for all deductible temporary differences, carried forward unused tax credit and unused 
tax losses, to the extent that it is probable that taxable profit will be available against which deductible temporary differences, 
carried forward unused tax credit and unused tax losses can be utilised, except:
•	 Where the deferred tax asset in respect of deductible temporary difference which arises from the initial recognition of an 
asset or liability which at the time of the related transaction, affects neither the accounting profit nor taxable profit or loss; 
and
•	 In respect of deductible temporarily differences associated with investments in subsidiaries and associates, deferred tax 
assets are recognised only to the extent that it is probable that the temporary differences will reverse in the foreseeable 
future and taxable profit will be available against which the temporary differences can be utilised.
The carrying amount of deferred tax assets is reviewed at each balance sheet date and reduced to the extent that it is no 
longer probable that sufficient taxable profit will be available to allow all or part of the deferred income tax asset to be utilised. 
Previously unrecognised deferred tax assets are re-assessed at each balance sheet date and are recognised to the extent that 
it has become probable that future taxable profit will allow the deferred tax assets to be recovered.
Deferred tax assets and liabilities are measured at the tax rates that are expected to apply in the year when the asset realised 
or the liability is settled based on tax rates and tax laws that have been enacted or substantively enacted at the balance sheet 
date.
Deferred tax is charged or credited to the consolidated income statement, except when it relates to items recognised directly 
to equity, in which case the deferred tax is also dealt with in the equity account.
Deferred tax assets and liabilities are offset when there is a legally enforceable right for the Group to offset current tax assets 
against current tax liabilities and when they relate to income taxes levied by the same taxation authority on:
•	 Either the same taxable entity; or

3.21 FINANCIAL INSTRUMENTS
Financial instruments – initial recognition and presentation
Financial assets
Financial assets within the scope of Circular No. 210/TT-BTC issued by the Ministry of Finance on 6 November 2009 providing 
guidance for the adoption in Vietnam of the International Financial Reporting Standards on presentation and disclosures of 
financial instruments (“Circular 210”) are classified, for disclosures in the notes to the consolidated financial statements, as 
financial assets at fair value through profit or loss, held-to-maturity investments, loans and receivables or available-for-sale 
financial assets as appropriate. The Group determines the classification of its financial assets at initial recognition.
All financial assets are recognised initially at cost plus directly attributable transaction costs.
The Group’s financial assets include cash and cash equivalents, short-term trade receivables, other receivables and 
investments.
Financial liabilities
Financial liabilities within the scope of Circular 210 are classified, for disclosures in the notes to the consolidated financial 
statements, as financial liabilities at fair value through profit or loss or financial liabilities measured at amortised cost as 
appropriate. The Group determines the classification of its financial liabilities at initial recognition.
All financial liabilities are recognised initially at cost, net of directly attributable transaction costs.
The Group’s financial liabilities include short-term trade and other payables, accrued expenses and loans.
Financial instruments – subsequent re-measurement
There is currently no guidance in Circular 210 in relation to subsequent re-measurement of financial instruments. 
Accordingly, the financial instruments are subsequently re-measured at cost.
Offsetting of financial instruments
Financial assets and financial liabilities are offset and the net amount reported in the consolidated balance sheet if, and only if, 
there is a currently enforceable legal right to offset the recognised amounts and there is an intention to settle on a net basis, 
or to realise the assets and settle the liabilities simultaneously.
3.22 SEGMENT INFORMATION
A segment is a component determined separately by the Group which is engaged in providing products or related services 
(business segment) or providing products or services in a particular economic environment (geographical segment), that is 
subject to risks and returns that are different from those of other segments.
3.23 RELATED PARTIES
Parties are considered to be related parties of the Group if one party has the ability to control the other party or exercise 
significant influence over the other party in making financial and operating decisions, or when the Group and other party are 
under common control or under common significant influence. Related parties can be enterprise or individual, including close 
members of the family of any such individual.

COVID-19 PANDEMIC
The Covid-19 pandemic is resulting in an economic slowdown and adversely impacting most businesses and 
industries. This situation may bring uncertainties and have an impact on the environment in which the Company operates. 
The Company’s management has continuously monitored ongoing developments and assessed the financial impact in respects of 
the valuation of assets, provisions and contingent liabilities, and has used estimates and judgement in respect of various 
issues as the situation has evolved, using the best information obtained up to the date of these separate financial statements.

31. CORPORATE INCOME TAX
The Group has the obligation to pay corporate income tax (“CIT”) at the rate of 20% of taxable profits. In addition, the Company’s 
subsidiaries are entitled to the following CIT exemption and reductions:
•	 At ABT: According to Circular No. 96/2015/TT-BTC dated 22 June 2015 issued by Ministry of Finance and Official Letter 
No. 2200/CT-THNVDT dated 18 November 2015 issued by Department of Taxation of Ben Tre Province, ABT is entitled to 
preferential CIT over the entire operating period applied to incomes from cultivating aquacultures in disadvantage areas. 
Accordingly, CIT tax rate applied for profit from cultivating aquacultures activities from 2015 is 10%.
•	 At Vinaseed: On 1 March 2011, Vinaseed was approved as a scientific and technological enterprise through the Certificate 
No. 03/DK-DNKHCN issued by the Department of Science and Technology of Hanoi. According to the current regulations on 
scientific and technological enterprise and CIT incentives, Vinaseed shall be entitled to CIT exemption and reduction as a 
newly established enterprise from investment in the sector of high-tech, scientific research and technological development 
if revenues generated from scientific and technological products and goods for the first, second and third year exceed total 
revenue by 30%, 50% and 70%, respectively. In particular:
(i)  The tax rate of 10% shall be applied for fifteen (15) years from the first-year generated revenue from scientific and technological 
activities; and
(ii)  Vinaseed shall be exempted from CIT for a period of four (4) years and entitled to a 50% reduction of CIT payable for the 
subsequent nine (9) years.
•	 At SSC: On 30 July 2012, SSC was approved as a scientific and technological enterprise through the Certificate No. 08/DK-
DNKHCN issued by the Department of Science and Technology of Ho Chi Minh City. According to the current regulations on 
scientific and technological enterprise and CIT incentives, SSC shall be entitled to CIT exemption and reduction as newly 
established enterprise from investment in the sector of high-tech, scientific research and technological development if 
revenues generated from scientific and technological products and goods for the first, second and third year exceed total 
revenue by 30%, 50% and 70%, respectively. In particular:
(i)  The tax rate of 10% shall be applied for fifteen years (15) from the first-year generated revenue from scientific and technological 
activities; and
(ii)  SSC shall be exempted from CIT for a period of four (4) years and entitled to a 50% reduction of CIT payable for the subsequent 
nine (9) years.
•	 At FMC: From the fiscal year ended 31 December 2015, the Company applied Circular No. 96/2015/TT-BTC dated 22 June 
2015 issued by Ministry of Finance of Vietnam providing guidelines for corporate income tax and the Official Letter No. 1327/
CT-TTr from Tax Department of Soc Trang Province on 1 December 2012. Details are as below:
(i)  For agricultural and seafood activities in extremely disadvantaged areas: the Company is entitled to corporate income tax 
(“CIT”) exemption over the entire period; and
(ii)  For seafood activities in disadvantaged areas: the Company is entitled to CIT at the rate of 10% over the entire period.
The other subsidiaries have the obligation to pay CIT at the rate of 20% of taxable profits.
The tax returns filed by Group are subject to examination by the tax authorities. As the application of tax laws and regulations 
is susceptible to varying interpretations, the amounts reported in the consolidated financial statements could change at a later 
date upon final determination by the tax authorities.

34. FINANCIAL RISK MANAGEMENT OBJECTIVES AND POLICIES
The Group’s principal financial liabilities comprise loans, trade and other payables. The main purpose of these financial 
liabilities is to finance the Group’s operations. The Group has loan, trade and other receivables, and cash and short-term 
deposits that arise directly from its operations. The Group also hold available-for-sale investments. The Group does not hold 
or issue derivative financial instruments.
The Group is exposed to market risk, credit risk and liquidity risk.
Management reviews and agrees policies for managing each of these risks which are summarised below.
MARKET RISK
Market risk is the risk that the fair value of future cash flows of a financial instrument will fluctuate because of changes in 
market prices. Market prices comprise four types of risk: interest rate risk, currency risk, commodity price risk and other 
price risk, such as equity price risk. Financial instruments affected by market risk include loans, deposits and available-for-
sale investments.
The sensitivity analyses in the following sections relate to the position as at 31 December 2020 and 31 December 2019.
The sensitivity analyses have been prepared on the basis that the amount of net debt, the ratio of fixed to floating interest rates 
of the debt and the proportion of financial instruments in foreign currencies are all constant.
In calculating the sensitivity analyses, management assumed that:
•	 the statement of the consolidated balance sheet relates to available-for-sale debt instrument; and
•	 the sensitivity of the relevant consolidated income statement item is the effect of the assumed changes in respective market 
risks. This is based on the financial assets and financial liabilities held at 31 December 2020 and 31 December 2019.
Interest rate risk
Interest rate risk is the risk that the fair value or future cash flows of a financial instrument will fluctuate because of changes 
in market interest rates. The Group’s exposure to market risk for changes in interest rate relates primarily to the Group’s 
cash and short-term deposits and borrowings. These investments are mainly short term in nature and they are not held for 
speculative purposes.
The Group manages interest rate risk by looking at the competitive structure of the market to obtain rates which are favourable 
for its purposes within its risk management limits.
Interest rate sensitivity
A sensitivity analysis is not performed for interest rate risk as the Group’s exposure to the interest-rate risk is minimal at the 
reporting date as the loans from banks are short-term with fixed interest rates.

Foreign currency risk
Foreign currency risk is the risk that the fair value or future cash flows of a financial instrument will fluctuate because of 
changes in foreign exchange rates. The Group’s exposure to the risk of changes in foreign exchange rates relates primarily to 
the Group’s operating activities (when revenue or expense is denominated in a different currency from the Group’s accounting 
currency).
The Group is exposed to foreign currency risk in relation to purchases and sales of goods which are denominated in currencies 
other than its accounting currency as disclosed in Note 2.4. The Group manages its foreign currency exposure by considering 
the prevailing and expected market situation when it plans for future purchases and sales of goods denominated in foreign 
currencies, other than increasing natural-hedged proportion. The Group does not employ any derivative financial instruments 
to hedge its foreign currency exposure.
Equity price risk
The Group’s listed and unlisted equity securities are susceptible to market price risk arising from uncertainty about future 
values of the investment securities. The Group manages equity price risk by placing a limit on equity investments. The Board 
of Directors reviews and approves all equity investment decisions.
CREDIT RISK
Credit risk is the risk that counterparty will not meet its obligations under a financial instrument or customer contract, leading 
to a financial loss. The Group is exposed to credit risk from its operating activities (primarily for trade receivables) and from its 
financing activities, including deposits with banks, foreign exchange transactions and other financial instruments.
Bank deposits
The Group’s bank balances are mainly maintained with well-known banks in Vietnam. The Group’s maximum exposure to 
credit risk for the components of the balance sheet at each reporting dates are the carrying amounts as illustrated in Notes 5. 
The Group evaluates the concentration of credit risk in respect to bank deposit as low.
Trade receivables
Customer credit risk is managed by the Group based on its established policy, procedures and control relating to customer 
credit risk management.
Outstanding customer receivables are regularly monitored. The requirement for impairment is analyzed at each reporting 
date on an individual basis for major clients. The Group seeks to maintain strict control over its outstanding receivables and 
has a credit control department to minimize credit risk. In view of the aforementioned and the fact that the Group’s trade re-
ceivables relate to a large number of diversified customers, there is no significant concentration of credit risk.
Except for the financial assets for which provision have been made as disclosed in Notes 7 and 8, management evaluate all 
financial assets are neither past due nor impaired as they related to recognized and creditworthy counterparties
LIQUIDITY RISK
The liquidity risk is the risk that the Group will encounter difficulty in meeting financial obligation due to shortage of funds. The 
Group’s exposure to liquidity risk arises primarily from mismatches of maturities of financial assets and liabilities.
The Group monitors its liquidity risk by maintain a level of cash and cash equivalents and bank loans deemed adequate by 
management to finance the Group’s operations and to mitigate the effects of fluctuations in cash flows.

•	 Fair value of quoted notes and bonds is based on price quotations at the reporting date.

Fresh glutinous and sweet corn varieties of PAN currently

Packaged rice 
Ban Mai Rice: Ban Mai rice is produced from purebred rice, 
which is a clean fresh rice product produced in a closed 
manner from the selection of good varieties, under strict 
management. Immediately after harvesting, the rice is 
transferred to the modern drying and processing system of 
VinaRice (in Dong Thap), ensuring 100% freshness. Ban Mai 
rice meets the VietGap standards, on a completely closed, 
modern Japanese processing line.
VJ Pearl, VJ Japonica: these varieties are grown from a 
strictly controlled seed stock and are cultivated, harvested, 
and processed using technologies developed for the 
Japanese market. These processing techniques ensure the 
maintenance of nutritional value and natural aroma.  
RVT rice: Vinaseed has identifed the most viable agricultural 
areas for mass production of RVT rice. In these areas, 
seed selection, soil preparation, and irrigation are strictly 
controlled. Postharvest processing is done using German 
and Japanese equipment to yield a product that meets the 
most stringent market requirements.
Special rice (red rice, black rice): these products are rich in 
bioactive substances, fiber, protein, vitamins, minerals, and 
micronutrients. These products protect the body’s ability to 
regulate blood pressure, control cardiovascular functions, 
and stabilize blood sugar levels.
Vinaseed’s ST24, ST25 rice
Vinaseed’s ST24, ST25 rice varieties uses purebred rice 
varieties which were provided by engineer Ho Quang Cua. 
These varieties are planted in the “rice-shrimp” cultivation 
areas. To be specific, Vinaseed’s ST24 and ST25 rice 
is produced in a closed “field to table” model utilizing 
“purebred rice varieties’’ produced using special symbiotic 
breeding and production methods that integrate with rice 
and shrimp farming at sites in Soc Trang, Bac Lieu and 
Ca Mau. Aside from this, the rice is processed, milled and 
packed using modern technology from Japan and Israel, and 
is produced under FSSC 22000 certification standards. This 
organic farming method gives the rice grain a bolder and 
more fragrant flavor. The ST24 and the ST25 have long, clear 
and silver-free grain. When cooked, they are still soft and 
fragrant despite cooling.  They contain double the amount of 
protein compared regular rice (10% protein).

1. GOVERNANCE 
STRUCTURE
In the production and business activities, The PAN Group’s Board of Directors and Board of 
Management have determined that risk management is one of the top corporate governance 
principles that need special attention. The Board of Directors has proposed and implemented 
many risk management measures to minimize the adverse effects of these risks on production 
and business activities. Aims of risk management:
•	 Timely identifying risks and exploiting opportunities, optimizing operational efficiency;
•	 Strengthening capacity in decision-making, planning, and prioritizing work based on a 
thorough and coherent understanding of the business operations, business environment, 
opportunities and challenges of the Group;
•	 Protecting and strengthening the assets as well as the image of the Group
•	 Delineating responsibilities for risk ownership and management, developing a mechanism 
for continuous risk monitoring and reporting throughout the Group
In 2021, the PAN Group will continue to maintain and operate risk management according to 
the established system, at the same time, continuing to upgrade the risk management system 
including its people, processes, softwares and the necessary equipment to ensure the best 
achievements of risk management goals, especially in the context of the Covid-19 pandemic 
still raging around the world and in danger of resurging at any time in Vietnam.
In addition to the individual insurance programs in each company according to the specific 
activities, The PAN Group also works with the AON insurance brokerage company to evaluate 
and propose suitable insurance programs.

“
Dear valued Shareholders,
In 
2021, 
the 
COVID-19 
pandemic 
significantly affected the socio-economic 
activities of every country in the world. 
Domestically, the wave of pandemic that 
broke out at the end of April with a new 
strain turned 2021 into one of the most 
difficult years of Vietnam’s economy since 
its opening. The pandemic spread caused 
production delays and supply chain 
disruptions on a large scale, especially in 
the third quarter. However, thanks to the 
drastic action of the Government and the 
cooperation of organizations, businesses, 
and people, the country successfully 
overcame the most difficult period. By 
the end of 2021, Vietnam’s GDP grew 
positively at 2.58% with a record total 
import and export turnover of USD 668.5 
billion, up by 22.6% compared to 2020.
Although many economic sectors suffered 
heavy 
losses, 
agricultural 
production 
was still maintained, contributing to 
ensuring social security and national food 
security as well as the growth of export 
turnover, clearly defined as one of the solid 
economic pillars in all circumstances. The 
agricultural industry in 2021 grew by 3.18%, 
and the total export turnover of agricultural, 
forestry, and fishery products reached a 
record high of over USD 48.6 billion.
Thanks to the spirit of proactive adaptation 
and especially solidarity, understanding, 
and sharing from leaders to employees in 
all units, The PAN Group turned “threats” 
into “opportunities”, together with each 
other to get through difficult times. By 
the end of 2021, the Group’s consolidated 
net revenue reached VND 9,249 billion, 
an increase of 11% compared to 2020. 
Consolidated profit after tax and profit 
after tax attributed to shareholders of 
the parent company were VND 511 billion 
and 296 billion, increased by 53.5% and 
57.4% respectively over the previous year. 
The business segments: seeds, agro-
pharmaceuticals, aquaculture, and nuts 
are the main contributors to sales growth 
and impressive business performance,

which was a testament to the sustainable

with modern, safe, and highly economic 
farming solutions. 
Core business expansion projects continued 
to be implemented: the constructions

bottling plants,... with an estimated total 
investment of over 600 billion VND.

shrimp breeding and shrimp feed. This 
is a strategic step to complete the value 
chain in the shrimp export segment, with 
the goal of seizing opportunities from the 
expanded market, especially the European 
market with the advantage of the EVFTA

Investing in agriculture and food is a journey 
that takes a lot of patience. The shift from a 
fragmented agriculture, mainly producing 
raw materials to an advanced agriculture 
with deep processing capacity, creating 
high value products requires gradual, 
continuous and durable improvements for 
many years. We have been and will always 
be persistent with this goal.

In 2021, the global supply chain was disrupted because 
production and freight activities cannot keep up with 
the increasing demand and the economic recovery. 
The entire supply chain was constricted at many places 
around the world. A strong outbreak of the pandemic 
in Southeast Asia in the third quarter of 2021 led to the 
mass closures of factories in this region. Congestion 
occured at some major seaports in China because of 
strict COVID-19 control measures. Chip shortage crisis 
happening due to the booming demand for technology 
equipment, the power shortage crisis in China, the 
lack of containers, the lack of cargo ships, the lack of 
truck drivers… caused the global supply chain to face 
numerous difficulties.
As a result of supply chain corruptions, sea freight 
rates skyrocketed. According to the Freightos Baltic 
Index (FBX), sea freight rates for a 40-foot container 
broke the record, hitting over USD 11,000 in September 
2021, equivalent to a nearly five-fold increase over the 
same period in 2020 and 10 times compared to pre-
pandemic period, greatly affecting business costs.
The global supply chain congestion, the expansionary 
monetary and fiscal policies of many countries in an 
effort to revive the economy resulted in an escalation of 
inflation. Along with the strong recovery of consumer 
demand, food prices and fuel prices also increased 
sharply. According to the Food and Agriculture 
Organization of the United Nations (FAO), the FAO Food 
Price Index reached its peak in a decade in November 
2021 with 134.4 points. By the end of 2021, the FAO 
Food Price Index averaged 125.7 points, a 28.1 percent 
increase over 2020.

Vietnam’s economy overcame difficulties in 2021
2021 was a challenging year for Vietnam’s economy. According 
to the General Statistics Office (GSO), Vietnam’s gross domestic 
product (GDP) increased by 2.58% compared to 2020, 0.33 
percentage points lower than the same period, due to the severe 
impact of the COVID-19 pandemic to all sectors of the economy. In 
particular, in the third quarter of 2021, prolonged social distancing 
in key economic areas such as Ho Chi Minh City, Binh Duong, Dong 
Nai, Ba Ria-Vung Tau, Long An, Hanoi, Bac Ninh, Bac Giang,..., 
caused the country’s GDP in the third quarter to decrease by 6.02% 
over the same period, an all-time low decrease in GDP growth 
rate. However, thanks to fast-track vaccination and adaptability 
to the pandemic in “The new normal”, Vietnam’s economy made 
an impressive recovery in the last quarter of 2021 with a recorded 
growth rate of 5.22% compared to the previous year.
Agriculture, forestry and fishery production took place in 
favorable weather conditions, with good crop and livestock 
productivity. However, the complicated pandemic situation 
affected the supply chain of agricultural, forestry and fishery 
products. Facing the intertwined advantages and difficulties, 
business performance in 2021 of the agriculture, forestry and 
fishery sector has clearly proved its supporting role in the 
economy with a growth rate of 2.9%, contributing 13.97% to the 
growth rate of total value added of the economy.
Industrial production in the fourth quarter of 2021 prospered right 
after localities across the country implemented the Government’s 
Resolution on “safe adaptation, flexibility, effectively controlling 
the Covid-19 pandemic”. The value-added of the industry in 2021 
increased by 4.82% compared to 2020 (1.5 percentage points 
higher compared to the increase in 2020). This growth rate of the 
industry in the midst of severe impacts of COVID-19 pandemic in 
Vietnam was a highlight, making remarkable contributions to the 
overall growth of the entire economy.
Trade activities and services were negatively affected by the 
complicated progress of the pandemic since the end of April 
2021. The negative growth rate of some major service industries 
led to the decline in overall growth rate of the service sector and 
the economy.

2. MAIN BUSINESS ACTIVITIES
2.1. 
AGRICULTURE SECTOR
The agriculture sector in 2021 took place in relatively favorable weather conditions for crops and 
livestock to grow and develop. However, due to the complicated development of the Covid-19 
pandemic, especially in the third quarter, many localities have implemented social distancing, 
affecting the supply chain of production – processing – consumption of agricultural products.
In a situation where both advantages and disadvantages were intertwined, the agriculture sector has 
had many timely response solutions, together with the effective implementation of the Government’s 
Resolution No.128/NQ-CP dated October 11, 2021 to stabilize and develop production, reaching a 
high growth rate. The performance results of the agricultural sector in 2021 have demonstrated 
the role of the pedestal of the economy, ensuring the supply of food and essential goods, to be the 
important base to implement welfare and security during the pandemic.
Rice production in the year achieved positive results. According to the General Statistics Office, 
rice area in 2021 estimated at 7.24 million hectares, a decrease of 38.3 thousand hectares over the 
previous year rice yield was 60.6 quintal/ha, rose by 1.8 quintals/ha; rice production was estimated 
at 43.88 million tons, increasing by 1.1 million tons.
Vietnam’s rice export also had a positive year. According to a report of the Ministry of Agriculture 
and Rural Development (MARD), the volume of rice exported this year is equivalent to 2020 with a 
value of about USD 3.27 billion, up by 4.8% compared to the previous year. Rice export price in 2021 
has reached USD 530/ton, up by 8% over the previous year. These show that Vietnam’s rice exports 
are on the right track to reduce volume and increase export value thanks to improving quality.
The structure of Vietnam’s rice exports continues to shift to fragrant and high-quality rice with 
higher selling prices and added value. Moreover, rice farmers and traders are also increasingly 
interested in improving quality, traceability and aiming to meet the strict standards of demanding 
markets such as the EU, Korea, and America.
According to the forecast of the Vietnam Food Association, despite the complicated development of 
the COVID-19 pandemic, commercial activities in the world cannot be disrupted but strengthened 
more sharply because consumer demand and stockpiling of food increase in response to the 
COVID-19 pandemic and rice is one of the items that countries have the most stockpiles of.
Especially, in the condition that production, business, and logistics activities have been reopened 
after the COVID-19 pandemic, it is forecasted that 2022 will still be a year of many opportunities 
for Vietnam’s rice exports, especially after the Government issued Resolution 128 providing 
temporary guidance on “Safe adaptation, flexibility and effective control of the COVID-19 pandemic” 
to stabilize the economy.
In addition, many businessmen in the rice industry also said that right from the beginning of the 
year, rice exports were very optimistic, signaling that this year’s rice exports will have a stronger 
breakthrough because of many supporting factors benefiting both businesses and rice farmers: 
World food demand and prices rise, business resilience increases, and especially Vietnamese 
businesses have gained more experience to flexibly respond to different scenarios and produce 
safety during the COVID-19 pandemic, ensuring supply for domestic consumption and exports.
In the long run, the potential of The PAN Group’s seed segment is very promising based on a solid 
R&D foundation and high competence in product development. The modern infrastructure system 
that has just been invested in the Center for Agricultural and Seed Processing Industry in Dong 
Thap province comes into stable operation with high capacity, which will contribute significantly 
to revenue growth in the short and long term.
In addition, in 2022, The PAN Group will consolidate all revenue and profit from VFG, with the 
expectation that VFG’s revenue will grow at least 50% compared to 2021 thanks to the distribution 
of 2 strategic products from Syngenta partner. The cooperation of NSC and VFG in The PAN Group’s 
agricultural value chain is also the driving force to create synergistic value for this segment.

2.2. AQUACULTURE SECTOR
2021 was considered a turbulent year for Vietnam’s seafood industry, especially in the second and third 
quarters. Due to the application of nationwide social distancing measures, Vietnam’s seafood industry 
recorded a decrease in production and exports compared to the same period in 2020. However, in the 
fourth quarter, when anti-epidemic measures were eased, the seafood industry recorded impressive 
recovery numbers and even increased sharply. As a result of the whole year of 2021, Vietnam’s seafood 
industry recorded USD 8.9 billion in export turnover, up by 6% compared to 2020.
The top 5 biggest seafood importers from Vietnam are the CPTPP members, the US, China, Hong 
Kong, the EU, and South Korea. These top 5 trade blocs have imported up to 81.7% of the total export 
turnover of the Vietnamese market. Our country’s seafood exports have recorded an impressive 
recovery thanks to seafood imports from these trade blocs. In November and December 2021, import 
turnover recorded a growth of 30 to 50% over the same period in 2020. This shows that the demand 
for Vietnamese seafood imports in these economic blocs is quite large and is not likely to be replaced 
by other sources.
In 2021, China’s Zero Covid policy caused a large number of containers to be stuck in this country due 
to the implementation of isolation measures, which directly pushed up the price of freight rates (the 
main type of transport for seafood) to a record high, which has been sustained throughout 2021. The 
high freight rates greatly affected the profits of Vietnamese seafood companies as transportation costs 
account for a large proportion of their cost structure. However, from the end of 2021, shipping prices 
have cooled off around the world, which was good for the profit of Vietnamese seafood exporters.
The two largest seafood export groups in 2021 will continue to be Shrimp and Pangasius. The shrimp 
industry in 2021 recorded an export value of USD 3.9 billion, up by 4% over the same period, in which 
white-leg shrimp was still the most interesting product, accounting for more than 76% of the industry’s 
total export turnover.

According to data from Vietnam Customs, shrimp exports for the whole year in 2021 were at about 
USD 3.9 billion, up by 4% compared to 2020. This is a positive and remarkable result of the industry 
when factories in the West (which account for more than 80% of the industry’s processing output) 
continuously recorded F0 Covid cases and had to moderate production and reduce output even 
down to 70% in some places. Vietnam’s shrimp exports to the US in 2021 reached over USD 1 
billion, up by 22% over the same period in 2020 (the shrimp market share in the US market has 
increased by 13%); shrimp exports to the EU reached USD 576.6 million, an increase of 17 % over 
the same period in 2020.
Other important markets for Vietnam’s shrimp exports are Japan and China, which account for 
about 25% of Vietnam’s total shrimp export turnover. In 2021, these were the two economies with 
relatively strict policies against the COVID-19 pandemic, constantly applying social distancing 
measures to control the spread of the virus. Moreover, regulations on the quarantine of imported 
products were also strictly adopted. As a result, Vietnam’s shrimp exports to Japan decreased 
by 5.7% over the same period in 2020 (especially in November and December, it plunged by 20%). 
In the Chinese and Hong Kong market, the shrimp industry recorded a drop of 21% over the same 
period in 2020 (however, in November and December, it recorded an increase of 19%).
In the whole year of 2021, the Vietnamese pangasius industry recorded an export turnover of USD 
1.6 billion, an increase of 8.4% over the same period in 2020. After 3 quarters of ups and downs, 
in Q4.2021, the value of Vietnamese pangasius exports to the Chinese market recorded a strong 
growth compared to the same period in 2020 (144.3 %). 2021 was considered a difficult year for 
Vietnam’s pangasius export industry when the industry’s main import markets which are China 
and Hong Kong continuously recorded a decrease in import output, due to their application of Zero 
Covid policies and continuous social distancing measures.
Another major market of Vietnam’s pangasius industry is the US, which recorded positive results 
from Q4.2021 and the whole of 2021 with a growth of 66.9% and 50.5% respectively. In 2021, the 
total value of pangasius exports to the US reached USD 370.6 million, double that of 2020. At the 
end of June 2021, The US Department of Commerce (DOC) has announced the final results of 
the 16th period of review (POR16) for the period from August 1, 2018 to July 31, 2019, regarding 
Vietnam’s pangasius exported to the US. Accordingly, the anti-dumping duty for two Vietnamese 
companies is USD 0 per kg, while the tax rate for other Vietnamese producers and exporters 
remained at USD 2.39 per kg. As a result, pangasius exports to this market grew continuously, 
which was foreseeable. Particularly in December 2021, the export value of pangasius to the US 
reached USD 46.6 million, up by 67% over the same period last year.
The seafood industry is expected to continue to have impressive growth in 2022. The reasons for 
it are the under controlled pandemic and the new Omicron variant that makes the symptoms of 
COVID-19 much milder and is not as dangerous to infected people as previous ones, which helps 
countries to ease their pandemic prevention measures so that consumption of aquatic foods can 
continue to be sustained and strongly recovered. Furthermore, it is expected that the reduction in 
sea freight rates will help businesses improve profits. Export prices are expected to remain the 
same or even increase slightly in 2022 as supplies continue to be constrained in major producing 
countries in the seafood industry such as India and Ecuador due to supply chain disruptions.
For the Company’s shrimp industry, newly invested factories are being constructed on schedule 
and are expected to be put into production in 2022. These new factories will help increase the 
Company’s output sharply. The autonomous pond system continues to improve in efficiency, 
helping the company get a better cost of goods sold in 2022.
For the pangasius industry, the Company successfully applied improvements in new production 
processes to reduce production costs and improve profit margins. In addition, the newly invested 
production systems will be put into operation in 2022.

The PAN Group is subject to the Group model in which the

At member companies with core production and business 
activities, the main investments are in projects of production, 
new factory constructions, capacity development, farming and 
processing area expansion,.... At the same time, M&A activities 
can also be carried out to expand market share or value chain, 
matching its business lines.
The Group’s strategic orientation in the period of 2020 - 2025 
is to focus on developing the core production capacity in each 
business segment on the available background; capitalizing 
the opportunities, if any, available at the market so that M&A 
of good companies may be initiated to be well matched with the

Reasons
VFC is a local leading manufacturer of agricultural materials, a very important chain in the 
agricultural production value chain to be developed and perfected by The PAN Group. VFC is recorded 
with a myriad of high potentials especially when comprehensive cooperation is initiated to capitalize 
the available advantages.  
Ģ	 Agro-chemical: VFC is characterized by over 25 years of experience, 7% of market shares, the

and trusted as reliable partner of many the world leading pharmaceutical manufacturers 
(Syngenta, Kumiai, Nippon, etc.) 
Ģ	 Fumigation (for agricultural product export): VFC is recorded with over 30 years of experience, 
60% of market shares, revenue of approximately VND 300 billion/ year (accounting for 11% of 
total revenue, making a contribution up to 22% of profit before tax), a member of International 
Maritime Fumigation Organization (IMFO) since 1999, awarding with the certificate of ISO 
9001:2000 BVQI-UKAS/ ANSI-RAB since 2001.  
Ģ	 VFC is supported by a nationwide distribution system and 16 VFC branches in provinces with 
over 2,500 agro-chemical agents (Tier 2), and 2,300 fumigation customers/agents.  
Ģ	 Long-lasting brand: VFC under agro-chemical, fumigation, and pest control perspectives 
refers to the great professionalism and prestige. VFC is prioritized rather than other rivals by 
the demanding exporters of agricultural products (EU, USA, and Japan market). 
Ģ	 VFC is the home of extensively experienced, and loyal managers, creating a reliable 
relationship with the agency and customer system, as a favorable condition to further 
develop the resonance strength between VFC and The PAN Group.

value of VND 658 billion. The PAN Group targeted an increase in owning the charter capital 
at VFC up to over 51% to consolidate VFC’s business results in the consolidated financial 
statements and scale up the Group.

REPORT FROM 
THE BOARD OF MANAGEMENT 
ON THE COMPANY’S BUSINESS 
PERFORMANCE IN 2021
1. BUSINESS OPERATION IN 2021
In 2021, The PAN Group had to deal with business difficulties when outbreaks of Covid-19 led to 
social distancing all over the country. The pandemic development was especially complicated in 
western provinces, severely affecting The Group’s seafood business activities. However, right 
from the end of the third quarter and beginning of the last quarter of 2021, when social distancing 
measures were eased, The Group’s business activities made a strong recovery to achieve 
impressive results in growth of net sales, an increase of 111%, equivalent to VND 9,249 billion for 
the whole year. Profit after tax was recorded at VND 511 billion, an increase of 41.8%.
In 2021, The Group completed the consolidation of Vietnam Fumigation Joint Stock Company 
(VFC), and restructured The Group system, turning all affiliates under PAN Food to be under 
ownership of The Group. After making a tender offer and successfully acquiring the ownership 
shares, The PAN Group officially holds 51.25% of VFG’s charter capital. VFC is a leading 
company in the field of agricultural materials production and trade, a very important link in the 
agricultural production value chain that The PAN Group is striving to build and complete. VFC has 
great potential, especially when it comes to comprehensive cooperation with The PAN Group to 
jointly realize existing advantages. The main strengths of VFC include: (i) VFC has a nationwide 
distribution system with 16 VFC branches in provinces, more than 2,500 agro-pharmaceuticals 
agents (tier 2) and 2,300 customers/ disinfection agents. ; (ii) VFC has a very experienced and 
long-term management team, establishing a strong connection with the system of agents and 
customers, which is a favorable factor to promote the synergistic advantages between VFC and 
The PAN Group and (iii) Long-standing brand: When it comes to VFC in agro-pharmaceuticals, 
fumigation, pest control, it is associated with professionalism and prestige. Customers exporting 
agricultural products to fastidious markets (EU, Japan, USA) prefer VFC to other firms.
Moreover, The Group made investment in FMC’s capital increase issuance along with Khang An 
Foods JSC, a company under FMC system in early 2021. FMC’s consolidated business results 
for the whole year of 2021 were recorded VND 5,199 billion, an increase of 17.8%. FMC with new 
investment in capacity increase and system development is expected to achieve rapid growth in 
2022, especially, revenue is projected to come from the US, a market that is having profound growth. 
In 2021, C.P Vietnam became a major shareholder by owning 24.9% of FMC’s charter capital. The 
cooperation with C.P. is expected to help FMC complete the supply chain of shrimp farming, which 
will bring great advantages to FMC when competing with companies in the same industry.

In the first 3 quarters of 2021, The Group had to face difficulties and declines in output and revenue 
when social distancing measures were enforced nationwide and especially in western provinces, 
the concentrated regions for most seafood products manufacturing activities of The Group. Social 
distancing measures also directly affected the packaged food segment, as purchasing power 
dropped markedly across the country. However, right in the fourth quarter, when distancing orders 
were eased and restrictions were lifted, The Group’s sales recovered quickly, the whole year net 
revenue was VND 9.2 trillion, an increase of 11.6%. Production and freight costs in the last quarter 
were significantly controlled and optimized, helping The Group’s EBITDA profit and profit after 
tax increase sharply, and total profit after tax increased by 53.3% at VND 511 billion. As a result, 
profitability ratios such as ROA, ROE and ROIC of The Group also improved in 2021.
Big contributors to The Group’s sales growth and business performance are the seafood sector, 
especially Sao Ta Foods Joint Stock Company (stock symbol: FMC) and Aquatex Bentre (stock 
symbol: ABT). With strong sales growth in US market as well as efficiency from autonomous 
farming areas, FMC recorded a revenue growth of 17% with sales reaching VND 5,200 billion; gross 
profit and profit after tax growth rates recorded at 23%. Meanwhile, ABT also had an impressive 
comeback to the pangasius industry when sales increased by only 4% but gross profit increased by 
73% compared to last year when the company successfully made improvements in the production 
procedures as well as benefited from sharp drop in the price of fish raw materials. The fishery 
industry is expected to achieve positive results in 2022 when capacity growth will be enhanced 
through new systems that are being completed and put into operation in early 2022. Export prices 
are also projected to remain high due to supply disruptions from other economies. Besides, the 
reduction in freight costs also helps the company achieve higher profit.
The Group’s agricultural sector is expected to grow well in 2022 with contributions from Vietnam 
Fumigation Joint Stock Company (stock symbol: VFG) and Vietnam National Seed Group JSC (stock 
symbol: NSC). On January 17th 2022, VFG officially signed a strategic cooperation agreement with 
Syngenta Vietnam, within the framework of cooperation, Syngenta and VFG committed to support 
each other to expand and develop business activities, making the best of potential of the market 
as well as maximizing strengths of each party. In 2021, NSC also recorded a growth rate of 16.45% 
compared to last year with improved business performance indicators. The company is currently 
developing and gradually increasing the proportion of the commercial rice segment in the revenue 
structure. NSC’s rice segment recorded revenue growth of more than 66% in 2021, benefiting from

Profit targets 
Are consolidated based on business results of the Parent Company and its subsidiaries on the basis of expected ownership ratio 
in 2022.
The profit plan in 2022, corresponding to the revenue plan, has significantly improved; largely from the increase in scale and profit margin 
in the seed and nut products segments. In addition, products in the shrimp and pangasius segment are also expected to have stable profit 
margins from favorable developments in the consumer market (although still negatively affected by the high logistics costs).
Consolidation of VFG will be a big push of growth for consolidated profit, as VFC itself also targets approximately 30% profit growth 
compared to 2021.
The Company’s orientation in 2022 will be: finding opportunities to merge good companies, staying in line with The PAN Group’s value 
chain, and most importantly, increasing ownership rate in companies with strong growth potential – like VFC. However, the Board of 
Directors draws this plan under careful consideration, and excluding the impact, if any, of the M&A deals the Company is pursuing.
PROFIT DISTRIBUTION PLAN 2022
Previously, revenue mainly came from Vinaseed’s plant seed and food business, from 2022 
the agricultural segment will have a large contribution from Vietnam Fumigation Joint Stock 
Company (VFC), regarding VFC’s official consolidation at the end of November 2021. VFC has its 
main revenue from the distribution of agrochemicals and disinfection and pest control services.
Future prospects of the agricultural sector are still focused on the overall recovery of the economy 
in Vietnam when Covid-19 pandemic almost no longer has a negative impact on production and 
business activities like it did in the period of 2020 - 2021. The high demand for food after recovery 
will be a good support for the business of both seeds and agrochemicals from 2022 onwards.
In the long term, the potential of The PAN Group’s seed business is very promising based on its 
solid R&D foundation and high competence in product development.
In addition to the prospect of a series of copyrighted rice varieties that will be introduced by 
Vinaseed from 2022, VFC’s agro-pharmaceutical business is also expected to have a breakthrough 
after strategic cooperation with Syngenta in distribution of products in the Vietnam market.
Along with that, a sustainable rice value chain from seed research to consumption of the final high 
quality rice product will bring more added value in the future. With the EVFTA taking effect from 
August 1, 2020, together with Vinarice’s FSSC22000 certification, The Group’s high-quality rice 
products are exported to high-end markets such as Europe and Australia.
The confectionery segment (BBC) is expected to have a good recovery thanks to the increase in 
domestic demand after the pandemic. Its revenue and profit are expected to grow and return to 
pre-epidemic levels. Meanwhile, nut export continues its high growth momentum from 2021, and 
production scale will expand in 2022 to meet the current high demand.
Meanwhile, seafood exports (FMC, ABT) will benefit from great demand from the US, European, 
Japanese markets, .. when these countries have opened their borders again before Vietnam and 
their economies are recovering strongly. FMC’s expanded factories that come into operation in 
2022 (Tam An, Sao Ta) will operate well because products are in high demand from the import 
markets of Europe, the U.S. and Japan. ABT and LAF will also plan to improve capacity of factories 
in 2022 to better satisfy customers’ needs.

safe, high quality and traceable agricultural and food products for domestic and international 
markets”. Growth from 2022 onwards is expected to reach a higher rate, coming from both 
core activities and expansion through M&A.

Resolution No. 16-07/2013/NQ-HĐQT of the BOD issued on July 15th, 2013 decided to establish 04 
Subcommittees to support the activities of the BOD including: Investment Subcommittee, Human 
Resources Subcommittee, Social Responsibility Subcommittee, Independent Administration 
Subcommittee. However, the Resolution of the 2014 Annual GMS approved the establishment of the 
Investment Council, with functions and duties as specified in Clause 3, Article 29 of the Charter of PAN 
Pacific Corporation, issued on October 28th, 2014. Accordingly, Resolution No. 15-06/2014/NQ-HĐQT 
canceled the contents related to Investment Subcommittee in the Company’s internal documents and 
dismissed Investment Subcommittee under the BOD.
On April 6th, 2015, the BOD approved the establishment of one more Subcommittee, which was 
Sustainable Development subcommittee under the BOD, to support the BOD in matters related to 
planning, consulting, monitoring, evaluating all sustainable development activities of the Company, 
focusing on 3 major issues: Economy, Environment and Society. The establishment of Sustainable 
Development Subcommittee was part of the strategy to professionalize environmental and social 
activities, fulfill corporate ethical obligations and aimed towards sustainable development in the future. 
Members of the subcommittee and coordinators at member companies were those who understood 
the company’s activities well, and had experience in social science issues. They also consulted, trained, 
and evaluated the various environmental, safety and social activities for large corporations in Europe, 
the United States, Japan, Korea... such as Sumitomo, Yamaha, CJ Vina, Palffiger, Levi Strauss (Levi’s)... 
Sustainable Development Subcommittee was established under Resolution No. 04-04/2015/NQ-HĐQT 
dated 06/04/2015.
Then, on April 24th, 2015, GMS of The PAN Group Joint Stock Company (at that time it was PAN Pacific 
Corporation) approved the cancellation of Investment Council and the removal of all provisions related 
and amended corresponding Charter, transferring all powers and obligations of Investment Council 
according to the current Charter to the BOD, according to Resolution No. 01-04/2015/NQ-ĐHĐCD dated 
24/04/2015, Article 7, Clause B.
On November 18th, 2018, the BOD of The PAN Group Joint Stock Company issued a resolution approving 
of personnel restructuring  of subcommittees under the BOD to meet the provisions of Decree 71/2017/ 
ND-CP on corporate governance, and Internal Regulations on corporate governance approved by the 
GMS on October 27, 2018. Specifically, the BOD approved the rename: from Subcommittee on Social 
Environment and Sustainable Development of the Company to Sustainable Development Subcommittee.
On September 29th, 2020, The PAN Group announced Resolution No. 02-09/2020/NQ-HĐQT of the BOD 
approving the establishment of Internal Audit Subcommittee and approving Internal Audit Regulations.
As of December 31, 2021, the Company had 04 Subcommittees under the BOD including Human 
Resources Subcommittee, Sustainable Development Subcommittee, Independent Subcommittee and 
Internal Audit Subcommittee.

SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES 
Cash and cash equivalents comprise cash on hand, cash at banks and short-term, highly liquid 
investments with an original maturity of less than three months that are readily convertible into 
known amounts of cash and that are subject to an insignificant risk of change in value.
Inventories are stated at the lower of cost incurred in bringing each product to its present location 
and condition, and net realisable value.
Net realisable value (“NRV”) represents the estimated selling price in the ordinary course of 
business less the estimated costs to complete and the estimated costs necessary to make the sale.
The perpetual method is used to record inventories, which are valued as follows:

Receivables are presented in the consolidated financial statements at the carrying amounts due 
from customers and other debtors, after provision for doubtful debts.
The provision for doubtful debts represents amounts of outstanding receivables at the balance 
sheet date which are doubtful of being recovered. Increases or decreases to the provision balance 
are recorded as general and administrative expense in the consolidated income statement.
Tangible fixed assets are stated at cost less accumulated depreciation.
The cost of a tangible fixed asset comprises its purchase price and any directly attributable costs 
of bringing the tangible fixed asset to working condition for its intended use.
Expenditures for additions, improvements and renewals are added to the carrying amount of the 
assets and expenditures for maintenance and repairs are charged to the consolidated income 
statement as incurred.
When tangible fixed assets are sold or retired, any gain or loss resulting from their disposal 
(the difference between the net disposal proceeds and the carrying amount) is included in the 
consolidated income statement.
Provision for obsolete inventories
An inventory provision is created for the estimated loss arising due to the impairment of value 
(through diminution, damage, obsolescence, etc.) of raw materials, finished goods, and other 
inventories owned by the Group, based on appropriate evidence of impairment available at the 
balance sheet date.
Increases or decreases to the provision balance are recorded into the cost of goods sold account 
in the consolidated income statement.

Intangible fixed assets are stated at cost less accumulated amortisation.
The cost of an intangible fixed asset comprises its purchase price and any directly attributable 
costs of preparing the intangible asset for its intended use.
Expenditures for additions, improvements are added to the carrying amount of the assets and 
other expenditures are charged to the consolidated income statement as incurred.
When intangible fixed assets are sold or retired, any gain or loss resulting from their disposal 
(the difference between the net disposal proceeds and the carrying amount) is included in the 
consolidated income statement.
Land use rights (“LURs”)
LURs are recorded as intangible fixed assets if the land is held for use in the production and

to Circular No. 45/2013/TT-BTC issued by the Ministry of Finance on 25 April 2013 providing 
guideline for the management, use and calculation of depreciation or amortisation of assets 
(“Circular 45”).
Copyrights
Copyrights of maize and rice varieties are recognized at the purchase price for varieties not 
researched and developed by the Group. Copyrights are amortized on a straight-line basis over 
the short period of time between the estimated useful life and the time of purchase.

11. Business combinations

12. Investments
Business combinations are accounted for using the purchase method. The cost of a business 
combination is measured as the fair value of assets given, equity instruments issued and liabilities 
incurred or assumed at the date of exchange plus any costs directly attributable to the business 
combination. Identifiable assets and liabilities and contingent liabilities assumed in a business 
combination are measured initially at fair values at the date of business combination.
Goodwill acquired in a business combination is initially measured at cost being the excess of the 
cost the business combination over the Group’s interest in the net fair value of the acquiree’s 
identifiable assets, liabilities and contingent liabilities. If the cost of a business combination is 
less than the fair value of the net assets of the subsidiary acquired, the difference is recognised 
directly in the consolidated income statement. After initial recognition, goodwill is measured at 
cost less any accumulated amortisation. Goodwill is amortised over 10-year period on a straight-
line basis. The parent company conducts the periodical review for impairment of goodwill of 
investment in subsidiaries. If there are indicators of impairment loss incurred is higher than the 
yearly allocated amount of goodwill on the straight-line basis, the higher amount will be recorded 
in the consolidated income statement.
Investments in associates
The Group’s investment in its associates is accounted for using the equity method of accounting. 
An associate is an entity in which the Group has significant influence that is neither subsidiaries 
nor joint ventures. The Group generally deems they have significant influence if they have over 
20% of the voting rights.
Under the equity method, the investment is carried in the consolidated balance sheet at cost plus 
post acquisition changes in the group’s share of net assets of the associates. Goodwill arising 
on acquisition of the associate is included in the carrying amount of the investment. Goodwill is 
not amortised and subject to annual review of impairment. The consolidated income statement 
reflects the share of the post-acquisition results of operation of the associates.
The share of post-acquisition profit/(loss) of the associates is presented on face of the 
consolidated income statement and its share of post-acquisition movements in reserves is 
recognised in reserves. The cumulative post-acquisition movements are adjusted against the 
carrying amount of the investment. Dividend receivable from associates reduces the carrying 
amount of the investment.
The financial statements of the associates are prepared for the same reporting period and use 
the same accounting policies as the Group. Where necessary, adjustments are made to bring the 
accounting policies in line with those of the Group.
Held-for-trading securities and investments in other entities
Held-for-trading securities and investments in other entities are stated at their acquisition costs.
Provision for diminution in value of investments
Provision of the investment is made when there are reliable evidences of the diminution in value 
of those investments at the balance sheet date. 
Increases or decreases to the provision balance are recorded as finance expense in the 
consolidated income statement.
Held-to-maturity investments
Held-to-maturity investments are stated at their acquisition costs. After initial recognition, held-
to-maturity investments are measured at recoverable amount. Any impairment loss incurred is 
recognised as finance expense in the consolidated income statement and deducted against the 
value of such investments.

Investment and development fund

by the weighted average number of ordinary shares outstanding during the period.

to ordinary equity holders of the Group by the weighted average number of ordinary shares 
outstanding during the period plus the weighted average number of ordinary shares that would be 
issued on conversion of all the dilutive potential ordinary shares into ordinary shares.

Payable and accrual are recognised for amount to be paid in the future for goods and services

19. Revenue recognition 
20. Taxation 
Revenue is recognised to the extent that it is probable that the economic benefits will flow to 
the Group and the revenue can be reliably measured. Revenue is measured at the fair value of 
the consideration received or receivable, excluding trade discount, rebate and sales return. The 
following specific recognition criteria must also be met before revenue is recognised:
Sale of goods
Revenue is recognised when the significant risks and rewards of ownership of the goods have 
passed to the buyer, usually upon the delivery of the goods.
Rendering of services
Where the contract outcome can be reliably measured, revenue is recognised by reference to the 
stage of completion. Stage of completion is measured by reference to the labour hours incurred 
to reporting date as a percentage of total estimated labour hours for each contract.
Interest
Revenue is recognised as the interest accrues (taking into account the effective yield on the asset) 
unless collectability is in doubt.
Dividends
Income is recognised when the Group’s entitlement as an investor to receive the dividend is 
established.
Income from transfer of trading securities
Income from the transfer of trading securities is determined as the difference between the selling 
price and the transferred cost price. This income is recognized on the transaction date, i.e., when 
the transfer contract is executed.

Current income tax
Current income tax assets and liabilities for the current and prior periods are measured at the 
amount expected to be recovered from or paid to the taxation authorities. The tax rates and tax 
laws used to compute the amount are those that are enacted as at the balance sheet date.
Current income tax is charged or credited to the consolidated income statement, except when it 
relates to items recognised directly to equity, in which case the current income tax is also dealt 
with in equity.
Current income tax assets and liabilities are offset when there is a legally enforceable right for 
the Group to offset current tax assets against current tax liabilities and when the Group intends to 
settle its current tax assets and liabilities on a net basis.
Deferred tax
Deferred tax is provided using the liability method on temporary differences at the balance 
sheet date between the tax base of assets and liabilities and their carrying amount for financial 
reporting purposes.

a preferential tax rate of 10%, CIT 
exemption for the first 4 years and a 50% 
reduction for the next 9 years.
